chapters.title: Semiconductors and Semiconductor Devices
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces semiconductors as a class of solids distinct from conductors and insulators, explaining their unique electrical properties and temperature-dependent conductivity. It covers intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, p-n junctions, and the working principles of semiconductor devices such as diodes and transistors.
key_concepts: Electric field and current density relationship

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This textbook covers the fundamental principles of semiconductors and semiconductor devices, building on prior knowledge of conductors and insulators. It explores the electrical properties of semiconducting materials, charge carrier behavior, and the operation of key semiconductor devices such as diodes and transistors.

events.text: j = sigma × E — more sigma, more current
More heat → more collisions → lower drift speed → lower sigma
Insulator: electrons locked, sigma ≈ zero
Semiconductor: some free electrons, sigma between conductor and insulator
Semiconductor: heating FREES more electrons → sigma RISES
Controllable conductivity = the foundation of all electronics
Atomic levels = fixed rungs (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s…)
N atoms → N split levels → energy band
Each atomic level → one energy band in a solid
Band gap = forbidden energy range
Current flows → electrons must move to slightly higher energy
Q: Find the electric field E that gives a conduction electron 1 eV of energy in copper. (Mean free path d = 4 × 10⁻⁸ m)
Force on electron = eE
Work done over distance d = eEd  (= energy transferred)
Energy transferred = eE × (4 × 10⁻⁸ m)
Set equal to 1 eV:   eE(4 × 10⁻⁸ m) = 1 eV
E = 2.5 × 10⁷ volts per meter
Q: A ten centimeter slab of diamond has a band gap of about six electron volts. What battery voltage is needed to drive current through it?
Electric field required ~ 10^7 V/m  (to supply ~6 eV to an electron, same order as in copper)
Slab thickness = ten centimeters = zero point one meters
Required battery voltage ≈ 10^6 V  (one million volts) — diamond is a perfect insulator.
Q: What is the thermal energy k T available to electrons at room temperature (three hundred kelvin)?
k T = (Boltzmann's constant) × 300 K
k T ≈ 0.026 eV
At room temperature (three hundred kelvin), k T is approximately zero point zero two six electron volts.
Q: Why is silicon classified as a semiconductor, given its band gap?
Band gap of silicon = one point one electron volts
Thermal energy at room temperature ≈ 0.025 eV  <<  band gap of insulators (~ 5 eV)
Silicon (band gap = one point one electron volts) has a small enough gap that thermal energy at room temperature excites a few electrons across it — making silicon a semiconductor, not an insulator.
Full band = no conduction; partially filled band = conductor
Si: 4 outer electrons → 4 covalent bonds
Silicon energy gap = 1.1 eV
Germanium gap = 0.68 eV
Broken bond → hole: a positive vacancy acting as a real charge carrier
Hole drifts opposite to electron flow
Q: Phosphorus is doped into silicon at a proportion of one in ten to the power of six. By what factor does the conductivity increase?
Dopant proportion: 1 in 10^6 phosphorus atoms in silicon
Conductivity increases by a factor of about 10^6 — matching the doping proportion exactly!
Q: How far below the conduction band is the impurity energy level for phosphorus in silicon?
Impurity: phosphorus in silicon → donor impurity levels form just below conduction band
E_gap (donor to conduction band) = 0.045 eV  (for P in Si)
Impurity level for P in Si: 0.045 eV below the conduction band — thermal energy is sufficient to excite donor electrons into conduction
Q: What energy is needed for a valence electron to fill the broken bond of an aluminium impurity in silicon, and what does this imply about the impurity energy level?
Energy needed to fill broken bond ≈ 0.057 eV
Electron jumps to impurity level → hole created in valence band
Acceptor impurity level = 0.057 eV above the valence band. Valence electrons jump up easily, creating holes in the valence band → p-type behaviour.
Q: What are the energy gaps for silicon and germanium, and what does this tell us about semiconductors?
Silicon energy gap = 1.1 eV
Germanium energy gap = 0.68 eV
Silicon: 1.1 eV gap
Thermal energy → breaks covalent bond
Free electron + hole = electron-hole pair
Generation ⇌ Recombination → steady state
Silicon at 300 K: n ≈ p ≈ 7 × 10¹⁵ per cubic metre
n-type: extra electrons from donor atoms
Q: Find the resistivity of an n-type semiconductor given: nₑ = 8×10¹³ cm⁻³, nₕ = 5×10¹² cm⁻³, μₑ = 2.3×10⁴ cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹, μₕ = 100 cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹
σ = e(nₑμₑ + nₕμₕ)
σ ≈ 2.94 C m⁻¹ V⁻¹ s⁻¹
ρ = 1/σ
n × p = constant for a given semiconductor
More heat → more electron-hole pairs → lower resistivity
More carriers → conductivity up, resistivity DOWN
Depletion region → built-in E field (n to p)
Q: Find the dynamic resistance of a p-n junction at (a) forward bias of one volt, and (b) forward bias of two volts.
(a) At V = 1 V, i = 10 mA; at V = 1.2 V, i = 15 mA
ΔV = 0.2 V, Δi = 5 mA
R = ΔV / Δi = 0.2 V / 5 mA = 40 Ω
(b) At V = 2 V, i = 400 mA; at V = 2.1 V, i = 800 mA
ΔV = 0.1 V, Δi = 400 mA
(a) Dynamic resistance at 1 V forward bias = 40 Ω
Q: Given a mobility value of two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb to the power of negative one, find the resulting resistivity.
rho = 1 / (2.94 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ C⁻¹)
rho ≈ 0.34 ohm-meters
Q: What is the average temperature coefficient of resistivity for silicon?
Silicon is a semiconductor → resistivity decreases as temperature increases
Therefore: temperature coefficient of resistivity α < 0
α (silicon) = negative zero point zero seven per kelvin
Q: In a rectifier circuit, the p-n junction is forward biased. Given that the junction resistance is much less than the load resistance R, what is the current through the load?
In forward bias: R_junction << R
So total resistance ≈ R (junction resistance is negligible)
i ≈ V zero divided by R, times sine of omega t plus phi
Q: Under what conditions does an LED emit visible light, and which semiconductor materials can produce it?
Silicon and germanium → photon wavelengths in the infrared (beyond 780 nm) → NOT visible
Compound semiconductors, e.g. gallium arsenide, indium phosphide → photon wavelengths inside 380 nm – 780 nm → visible light emitted
Visible LEDs require photon wavelength in 380 nm – 780 nm; achievable with compounds such as gallium arsenide or indium phosphide — NOT with silicon or germanium (infrared)
p-n junction = one-way gate; forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks
n-p-n: emitter (n, heavy)
EB junction: forward biased
I_E = I_B + I_C
Q: Given that IB is about one to five percent of IE, find the typical ranges of alpha and beta for a transistor.
alpha = IC / IE
IC = IE − IB ≈ 0.95 × IE  to  0.99 × IE
beta = IC / IB
beta = IC / IB ≈ IE / (0.01 to 0.05) × IE  →  beta ≈ 20 to 100
alpha ≈ 0.95 to 0.99
Q: Show that beta = alpha divided by (1 minus alpha), using Kirchhoff's current law IE = IB + IC.
Start: IE = IB + IC
Divide throughout by IC: IE/IC = IB/IC + 1
1/alpha = 1/beta + 1
1/beta = 1/alpha − 1 = (1 − alpha)/alpha
beta = alpha / (1 − alpha)

Q: A transistor amplifier has a load resistance R L in the collector circuit. The current gain is defined as delta I C divided by delta I B, and is typically of the order of fifty. What is the change in output voltage across R L?
Current gain = delta I C / delta I B ≈ 50
Change in output voltage: delta V = R L × delta I C
delta V = R L × delta I C, with current gain delta I C / delta I B of order fifty
Q: Find the voltage gain, current gain, and power gain of a common-emitter amplifier in terms of beta, RL, and RBE.
ΔI_B = v_i / R_{BE}
ΔI_C = β · ΔI_B = β · v_i / R_{BE}
v_o = R_L · ΔI_C = β · v_i · R_L / R_{BE}
Voltage Gain = v_o / v_i = β · R_L / R_{BE}
Current Gain = ΔI_C / ΔI_B = β
Power Gain = Voltage Gain × Current Gain = β² · R_L / R_{BE}
Voltage Gain = β·RL/RBE
Q: An LC network in a transistor oscillator has inductance L and capacitance C. Find the resonant frequency, and state how it can be varied.
omega_0 = 1 / (2π √(LC))
where L = inductance of the inductor, C = capacitance of the capacitor
Resonant frequency: omega_0 = 1 / (2π √(LC)). Frequency can be varied by varying L or C.
beta = I_C divided by I_B
Small I_B controls large I_C — current gain beta = I_C / I_B
0 = off / false / open, 1 = on / true / closed
AND: output is 1 only when BOTH inputs are 1
AND truth table: 1,1 → 1 only
OR: output is 1 when ANY input is 1
OR truth table: 0,0 → 0 only
NOT: output is the opposite of input
NOT truth table: 0→1, 1→0
Q: Write the truth table for Z = (X AND Y) OR X
X

Truth Table for Z = (X AND Y) OR X:
X=0, Y=0 → Z=0
X=0, Y=1 → Z=0
X=1, Y=0 → Z=1
X=1, Y=1 → Z=1
Q: Construct the truth table for X of A and B, where an OR gate and an AND gate are combined as shown.
Y = A OR B  (output of the OR gate)
X = A AND (A OR B)
A
Q: Two NOT gates feeding A and B, then a NAND gate — does the output equal A OR B?
Columns: A
A=0, B=0 → NOT A=1, NOT B=1 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=1 → Output = 0
A=0, B=1 → NOT A=1, NOT B=0 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=0 → Output = 1
A=1, B=0 → NOT A=0, NOT B=1 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=0 → Output = 1
A=1, B=1 → NOT A=0, NOT B=0 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=0 → Output = 1
Output is 0 only when both A = 0 and B = 0; output is 1 for all other combinations.
NOT(NOT A AND NOT B) = A OR B  — the circuit behaves as an OR gate
Q: Add two one-digit binary numbers A and B. Find the carry digit C and sum digit S for all combinations.
A=1, B=1 → C=1, S=0  (since 10 in binary = 2 in decimal)
Carry: C = A AND B
Sum: S = A XOR B = (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B)
C = A AND B
AND needs ALL ones. OR needs ANY one. NOT flips the input.
Billions of these gates, combined, = every computer ever made.

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_1>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's something strange: silicon, the material inside every smartphone and computer chip, conducts electricity better when you heat it up — but copper, the material in your wiring, conducts worse when you heat it. Same universe, opposite behaviour. Why? <<FOCUS:conductor-band>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_1:conductivity_spectrum>> <<SECTION:Conductors — a quick reminder|id=sec-1>>Let's start with what we know. In a conductor like copper, electrons are barely clinging to their atoms. They wander freely everywhere, like a crowd milling around in a huge open hall. <<FOCUS:copper-marker>> Apply an electric field inside that conductor, and all those free electrons feel a force and start drifting together. That drift of charge is electric current. <<WRITE_TEXT:j = sigma × E — more sigma, more current|id=text-1>>The conductivity sigma tells us how easily current flows — bigger sigma, better conductor. The current density — how much charge flows per unit area — is directly proportional to the electric field we apply. The constant of proportionality is conductivity, sigma. Bigger sigma means more current for the same push. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{j} = \sigma \vec{E}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now, what happens when we heat up copper? The atoms vibrate more violently, and the free electrons keep crashing into them. Each collision interrupts their drift. <<WRITE_TEXT:More heat → more collisions → lower drift speed → lower sigma|id=text-2>>So sigma falls, and resistivity — the resistance per unit length — goes up. <<POINT:temp-up-conductor-arrow>> <<FOCUS:insulator-band>> At the other extreme, insulators like rubber or glass have electrons that are tightly locked to their nuclei. No free electrons, almost no current — sigma is tiny, even with a strong electric field. <<WRITE_TEXT:Insulator: electrons locked, sigma ≈ zero|id=text-3>> Resistivity is just the flip side of conductivity. If conductivity tells you how easy it is to push current through, resistivity tells you how hard it is. One is the reciprocal of the other. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:semiconductor-band>> <<SECTION:Semiconductors — the middle ground|id=sec-2>>So where does silicon fit? Right in the middle. <<WRITE_TEXT:Semiconductor: some free electrons, sigma between conductor and insulator|id=text-4>>It has some free electrons — far fewer than copper — so it conducts a little, but nowhere near as well as a metal. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the big question: what happens when we heat up silicon? In copper, heating HURT conduction. So should silicon also get worse? <<POINT:silicon-marker>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Semiconductor: heating FREES more electrons → sigma RISES|id=key-1>>Actually, the opposite happens. In silicon, the electrons are weakly bound — not totally free, not totally locked. When you add heat, some of those weakly-bound electrons gain enough energy to break free. So the number of free electrons increases, and conductivity goes UP. <<POINT:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:temp-up-conductor-arrow>> Look at the spectrum: copper is way over on the right with enormous conductivity that falls with heat. Silicon sits in the middle with a conductivity that rises with heat. These two arrows point in opposite directions — that's the defining signature of a semiconductor. <<POINT:temp-up-conductor-arrow>> <<SECTION:Why this matters|id=sec-3>>This temperature-sensitive conductivity is not a bug — it's the feature. It means we can control how well silicon conducts by adding tiny amounts of other atoms, or by heating it, or by shining light on it. <<WRITE_KEY:Controllable conductivity = the foundation of all electronics|id=key-2>>That controllability is exactly what makes semiconductors the foundation of every transistor, diode, and chip ever built. <<TRACE:semiconductor-band>> <<PAUSE:short>> So the paradox we started with has a clean answer: copper gets worse when heated because more collisions slow the electrons that are already free. Silicon gets better when heated because heat frees more electrons in the first place. Same physics — energy and electrons — but a completely different starting point. <<POINT:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<POINT:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_2>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Why can copper carry electricity but a diamond — also full of electrons — absolutely refuses? Both materials are packed with electrons. So what is the secret difference? The answer lives not in the electrons themselves, but in the energy they are ALLOWED to have. <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:isolated-level>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_2:band_formation>> <<SECTION:Electrons in an isolated atom|id=sec-1>>Let's start with a single sodium atom sitting alone in space. Its electrons can only have certain fixed energies — one-s, two-s, two-p, three-s, and so on. Think of these as rungs on a ladder: an electron MUST sit on a rung. It cannot float between rungs. <<WRITE_TEXT:Atomic levels = fixed rungs (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s…)|id=text-1>>Sodium has eleven electrons. The inner levels — one-s, two-s, two-p — are completely filled. The outermost level, three-s, holds only one electron even though it could hold two. Everything above three-s is empty. <<POINT:isolated-level>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:n_atoms|to=3.0|from=1.0|duration=1800>> <<FOCUS:split-levels-few>> <<SECTION:Levels split into bands|id=sec-2>>Now bring a second sodium atom close. Suddenly those two three-s electrons can sense each other. The Pauli exclusion principle says no two electrons can share the same quantum state — so the single three-s level is FORCED to split into two slightly different energies. <<ANIMATE_PARAM:n_atoms|to=50.0|from=3.0|duration=2500>> <<FOCUS:band-region>> <<WRITE_TEXT:N atoms → N split levels → energy band|id=text-2>>Keep adding atoms — three, ten, a billion. Each new atom forces the level to split once more. By the time you have N atoms forming a solid, that single sharp three-s rung has split into N levels so densely packed they blur into a continuous smear. We call that smear an ENERGY BAND. <<PAUSE:short>> The total width of an energy band grows with the number of atoms N and how strongly they interact — the more atoms, the broader the smear of allowed energies. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E_{\text{band}} \approx N \times \Delta E_{\text{split}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each atomic level → one energy band in a solid|id=key-1>>This is the key idea: every atomic energy level becomes an energy band when atoms crowd together. The width of the band tells you how strongly those atoms are interacting. <<POINT:band-region>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:band-gap-region>> Now notice the gap between the three-s band and the three-p band above it. No allowed energy levels exist there — electrons are FORBIDDEN from having those energies. We call this the band gap, and it turns out to be the single most important feature of any solid. <<FOCUS:filled-half-marker>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Band gap = forbidden energy range|id=text-3>>Above the gap sits the three-p band — in sodium, completely empty. Below the gap is the three-s band — in sodium, only HALF full, because each sodium atom contributed just one electron to fill half of the available two-N states. <<POINT:filled-half-marker>> <<FOCUS:band-region>> Here is the question that connects everything: if you apply a voltage, why can an electron in a half-filled band accelerate, but an electron in a completely filled band cannot? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Current flows → electrons must move to slightly higher energy|id=text-4>>To carry current, an electron needs to speed up — gain a tiny bit of energy. In a HALF-FILLED band, empty levels are right next door at almost the same energy. The electron just hops up a fraction. Easy. <<POINT:filled-half-marker>> <<FOCUS:band-gap-region>> But in a COMPLETELY FILLED band, every level is occupied. There is nowhere to go — the Pauli principle blocks every adjacent slot. To move at all, the electron would need to leap across the entire band gap into the empty band above. If that gap is large, almost no electron can make that jump. The solid is an insulator. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter — Example forty five point one. We have a copper block, and we know that the mean free path of conduction electrons in copper is about four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. The question asks: what electric field is needed to give, on average, one electron volt of energy to a conduction electron? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the electric field E that gives a conduction electron 1 eV of energy in copper. (Mean free path d = 4 × 10⁻⁸ m)|id=ex-q-1>> Let's set up the physics. We call the electric field E. The force on the electron in that field is e times E, where e is the electron's charge. Now, as the electron moves through a distance d, the work done on it is force times distance — that is, e times E times d. This work equals the energy transferred to the electron. <<WRITE_STEP:Force on electron = eE|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Work done over distance d = eEd  (= energy transferred)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Before each collision, the electron travels an average distance equal to the mean free path — four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. So the energy transferred in one free path is e times E times four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. We want this to equal one electron volt. <<WRITE_STEP:Energy transferred = eE × (4 × 10⁻⁸ m)|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Set equal to 1 eV:   eE(4 × 10⁻⁸ m) = 1 eV|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now we solve for E. The e on the left cancels with the electron volt on the right — one electron volt is just one e times one volt — so we get E equals one volt divided by four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 1 V ÷ (4 × 10⁻⁸ m)|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<PAUSE:short>> Let's do that division: one divided by four times ten to the negative eight is two point five times ten to the power of seven. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 2.5 × 10⁷ V/m|id=ex-step-1-6>> And there's our answer. The required electric field is two point five times ten to the power of seven volts per meter. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 2.5 × 10⁷ volts per meter|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> Think about how enormous that is — two point five times ten to the seven volts per meter just to give a single electron one electron volt of energy. This is precisely why materials with large band gaps behave as insulators under ordinary voltages: the fields you'd need to push electrons across the gap simply aren't available in everyday conditions. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A ten centimeter slab of diamond has a band gap of about six electron volts. What battery voltage is needed to drive current through it?|id=ex-q-1>> Diamond's band gap — the energy gap between its highest filled band and the lowest empty band — is about six electron volts. The question is: how large a voltage would you actually need to push an electron across that gap through a real slab of material? To get an electron the energy it needs, the electric field inside the material has to be strong enough to supply six electron volts over the distance the electron travels. <<WRITE_STEP:Electric field required ~ 10^7 V/m  (to supply ~6 eV to an electron, same order as in copper)|id=ex-step-1-1>> From a companion example in the textbook, the electric field needed to supply six electron volts of energy to an electron is of the order of ten to the power of seven volts per meter. We assume the same value holds for diamond. Now we apply that field across our slab. <<WRITE_STEP:Slab thickness = ten centimeters = zero point one meters|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:V = E × d = (10^7 V/m) × (0.1 m) = 10^6 V|id=ex-step-1-3>> Voltage equals field strength times distance — ten to the power of seven volts per meter multiplied by zero point one meters — which gives ten to the power of six volts. <<PAUSE:short>> That is one million volts just to get a response from a single electron. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Required battery voltage ≈ 10^6 V  (one million volts) — diamond is a perfect insulator.|id=ex-ans-1>> This is why diamond is a perfect insulator: no ordinary battery could ever supply one million volts across a ten centimeter piece of diamond. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the thermal energy k T available to electrons at room temperature (three hundred kelvin)?|id=ex-q-1>> The textbook asks us to find k T at room temperature, which it defines as three hundred kelvin. This gives us a feel for the energy scale electrons are working with — and whether that's enough to jump a band gap. We evaluate k T by plugging in Boltzmann's constant and T equals three hundred kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:k T = (Boltzmann's constant) × 300 K|id=ex-step-1-1>> The product of those two numbers comes out to an energy in joules, but we convert to electron volts because that's the natural unit for band gaps in semiconductors. <<WRITE_STEP:k T ≈ 0.026 eV|id=ex-step-1-2>> And there's our answer. <<WRITE_ANSWER:At room temperature (three hundred kelvin), k T is approximately zero point zero two six electron volts.|id=ex-ans-1>> This is a crucially small number. Most semiconductor band gaps are on the order of one electron volt or more — meaning the thermal energy available at room temperature is roughly forty times smaller than a typical band gap. That's exactly why pure semiconductors conduct so poorly at room temperature: ordinary thermal jostling can only promote a tiny fraction of electrons across the gap. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why is silicon classified as a semiconductor, given its band gap?|id=ex-q-1>> The material in question is silicon, and the key fact the textbook gives us is that silicon has a band gap of one point one electron volts. Now, let's think about what that number means. <<WRITE_STEP:Band gap of silicon = one point one electron volts|id=ex-step-1-1>> The thermal energy available to electrons at room temperature is only around zero point zero two five electron volts — far less than the band gap of most insulators, which can be five electron volts or more. <<WRITE_STEP:Thermal energy at room temperature ≈ 0.025 eV  <<  band gap of insulators (~ 5 eV)|id=ex-step-1-2>> But silicon's band gap of one point one electron volts is comparatively small, so a modest amount of thermal energy is enough to push at least a few electrons across it. And that is exactly the conclusion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silicon (band gap = one point one electron volts) has a small enough gap that thermal energy at room temperature excites a few electrons across it — making silicon a semiconductor, not an insulator.|id=ex-ans-1>> Because the band gap of silicon is one point one electron volts, thermal excitation at room temperature is sufficient to promote a small but significant number of electrons into the conduction band, giving silicon its characteristic semiconducting behaviour. <<WRITE_KEY:Full band = no conduction; partially filled band = conductor|id=key-2>>So the answer to our diamond-versus-copper puzzle: copper's outermost band is half-filled — electrons roam freely. Diamond's filled band is separated from the empty band above by a huge gap of about five point five electron volts. Electrons are stuck. No current flows. <<POINT:upper-band-region>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So to summarise: when N atoms come together, each sharp atomic level fans out into a band of N levels. Whether that band is full or partly full — and how large the gap above it is — decides everything about whether a material is a metal, an insulator, or something in between. That in-between case is exactly what we will explore next: the semiconductor.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_3>>
Here's something strange: silicon is an insulator at absolute zero — zero charge carriers, zero current. Heat it up just a little, and it starts conducting. How does warmth create electricity? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_3:silicon_lattice>> <<SECTION:Silicon's Covalent Lattice|id=sec-1>>Let's look inside silicon. Each silicon atom has four outer electrons, and it shares one with each of its four neighbours to form covalent bonds. <<WRITE_TEXT:Si: 4 outer electrons → 4 covalent bonds|id=text-1>>Every electron in every bond sits in the valence band — locked in place, unable to carry current. <<TRACE:si-atom-grid>> <<FOCUS:broken-bond-site>> Now, at room temperature, atoms are constantly jiggling — thermally vibrating. Occasionally, one of those vibrations is violent enough to give a valence electron the energy it needs to break free of its bond entirely. <<SECTION:The Energy Gap|id=sec-2>>How much energy does that electron need? For silicon, the gap between the valence band and the conduction band is one point one electron volts. <<WRITE_KEY:Silicon energy gap = 1.1 eV|id=key-1>>That gap is small enough that ordinary thermal energy — room-temperature heat — can occasionally bridge it. <<POINT:free-electron>> <<PAUSE:short>> The energy gap is the minimum energy an electron needs to jump from the valence band into the conduction band — for silicon that's one point one electron volts, for germanium it's zero point six eight electron volts. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E_{\text{gap}}(\text{Si}) = 1.1\,\text{eV}, \quad E_{\text{gap}}(\text{Ge}) = 0.68\,\text{eV}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Germanium's gap is even smaller — just zero point six eight electron volts — which is why germanium conducts more readily at the same temperature. <<WRITE_TEXT:Germanium gap = 0.68 eV|id=text-2>>The smaller the gap, the easier thermal energy can knock electrons free. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:broken-bond-site>> So the electron escapes — it's now in the conduction band, free to wander from nucleus to nucleus and carry current. But here's the question I want you to think about: what's left behind at the broken bond? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:hole-marker>> <<SECTION:The Hole|id=sec-3>>A vacancy. An empty spot where an electron used to be. And because the surrounding lattice is electrically neutral except for this missing negative charge, that vacancy behaves as if it has a positive charge. We call it a hole. <<WRITE_KEY:Broken bond → hole: a positive vacancy acting as a real charge carrier|id=key-2>> <<POINT:hole-marker>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now watch what happens next. A neighbouring electron — still in its own bond — can slip over and fill this vacancy. The vacancy then appears one bond over. Then another electron fills that, and the vacancy hops again. <<TRACE:hole-drift-arrow>> Even though it's always electrons that are actually moving, the vacancy — the hole — appears to drift in the opposite direction, as if a positive particle were flowing through the crystal. <<WRITE_TEXT:Hole drifts opposite to electron flow|id=text-3>>That's two charge carriers from one broken bond: one conduction electron, one hole. <<POINT:hole-drift-arrow>> <<POINT:hole-drift-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example straight from the chapter on semiconductors. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Phosphorus is doped into silicon at a proportion of one in ten to the power of six. By what factor does the conductivity increase?|id=ex-q-1>> We have phosphorus being introduced into silicon — and the proportion is just one phosphorus atom for every ten to the power of six silicon atoms. That is an almost unimaginably tiny amount of impurity. Now, you might expect such a minuscule proportion of phosphorus — one part in ten to the power of six — to have a negligible effect on the material. <<WRITE_STEP:Dopant proportion: 1 in 10^6 phosphorus atoms in silicon|id=ex-step-1-1>> But phosphorus is a donor impurity, meaning each phosphorus atom donates a free electron that silicon itself cannot provide. Even at this vanishingly small concentration, those extra free electrons dramatically change how easily current can flow through the material. And the result is remarkable. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Conductivity increases by a factor of about 10^6 — matching the doping proportion exactly!|id=ex-ans-1>> The conductivity increases by a factor of about ten to the power of six. So a proportion of one in ten to the power of six produces a conductivity boost of ten to the power of six. This is the key lesson about doping: semiconductors are extraordinarily sensitive to even trace amounts of impurity, and that sensitivity is exactly what makes them so useful in electronics. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How far below the conduction band is the impurity energy level for phosphorus in silicon?|id=ex-q-1>> We're looking at what happens when phosphorus is introduced as a donor impurity into silicon. The key question is: how much energy separates those extra donor electrons from the conduction band? When phosphorus atoms sit inside a silicon crystal, each one donates an extra electron that doesn't quite belong to any one bond. These electrons occupy what we call impurity levels — energy states that are created by the dopant, sitting just inside the gap. <<WRITE_STEP:Impurity: phosphorus in silicon → donor impurity levels form just below conduction band|id=ex-step-1-1>> The critical thing is just how close those levels are to the conduction band edge. The textbook tells us that for phosphorus in silicon, the impurity level sits only zero point zero four five electron volts below the conduction band. <<WRITE_STEP:E_gap (donor to conduction band) = 0.045 eV  (for P in Si)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Compare that to the full silicon band gap of about one point one electron volts — this impurity level is extremely close to the top. Room-temperature thermal energy, which is roughly zero point zero two five electron volts, is almost enough on its own to bridge that tiny gap. <<PAUSE:short>> So in practice, at room temperature, virtually all of the donor electrons are thermally excited up into the conduction band and are free to conduct. And so the answer is: the donor impurity level for phosphorus in silicon is just zero point zero four five electron volts below the conduction band — so close that ordinary thermal energy is sufficient to promote those electrons into the conduction band, making phosphorus-doped silicon an effective n-type conductor. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Impurity level for P in Si: 0.045 eV below the conduction band — thermal energy is sufficient to excite donor electrons into conduction|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're looking at aluminium as an impurity in silicon — a classic p-type dopant. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What energy is needed for a valence electron to fill the broken bond of an aluminium impurity in silicon, and what does this imply about the impurity energy level?|id=ex-q-1>> Now, aluminium has only three outer electrons, but silicon needs four bonds with each neighbour. So the aluminium atom leaves one bond broken — it simply doesn't have that fourth electron to contribute. The broken bond between the aluminium atom and its fourth silicon neighbour can be filled by a nearby valence electron — but only if that electron picks up a little extra energy. <<WRITE_STEP:Energy needed to fill broken bond ≈ 0.057 eV|id=ex-step-1-1>> That amount is about zero point zero five seven electron volts — a very small energy compared to the full band gap of silicon, which means this process happens quite readily at room temperature. When a valence electron jumps up to fill that broken bond, it leaves behind a vacancy in the valence band — we call that vacancy a hole. <<WRITE_STEP:Electron jumps to impurity level → hole created in valence band|id=ex-step-1-2>> So we say that acceptor impurity levels are created just above the valence band, sitting only zero point zero five seven electron volts above it for aluminium in silicon. <<PAUSE:short>> Because this gap is so tiny, valence electrons can easily make the jump, and the material ends up with an abundance of holes as its primary charge carriers. And the answer is: the impurity levels for aluminium in silicon lie zero point zero five seven electron volts above the valence band. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Acceptor impurity level = 0.057 eV above the valence band. Valence electrons jump up easily, creating holes in the valence band → p-type behaviour.|id=ex-ans-1>> This tiny energy separation is what makes aluminium an effective p-type dopant — holes are generated with very little thermal energy required. Here's an example straight from the chapter on semiconductors. The textbook highlights two common semiconductor materials — silicon and germanium — and tells us the size of their energy gaps, that is, the gap between the valence band and the conduction band. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What are the energy gaps for silicon and germanium, and what does this tell us about semiconductors?|id=ex-q-1>> For silicon, the energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band is one point one electron volts. For germanium, that same gap is zero point six eight electron volts. <<WRITE_STEP:Silicon energy gap = 1.1 eV|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Germanium energy gap = 0.68 eV|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now, compare these to a true insulator — diamond, for instance, has an energy gap of around five point five electron volts. The gaps for silicon and germanium are dramatically smaller, which means electrons don't need nearly as much energy to jump up into the conduction band and carry current. And that is the key takeaway. Because the energy gap is small — one point one electron volts for silicon and zero point six eight electron volts for germanium — these materials sit in a sweet spot: they're not good conductors at very low temperatures, but at room temperature, thermal energy is just enough to kick some electrons across the gap. That's what makes them semiconductors rather than insulators. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silicon: 1.1 eV gap | Germanium: 0.68 eV gap → small gap enables semiconducting behavior|id=ex-ans-1>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So the more thermal energy the silicon has, the more bonds break, the more electron-hole pairs are created, and the more current it can carry. That's why conductivity rises with temperature in a semiconductor — the exact opposite of a metal. To tie it all together: a semiconductor sits between conductor and insulator because its energy gap is small but not zero. Silicon's one point one electron volt gap means heat can bridge it, freeing electrons and creating holes — both carry charge, both matter.

<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> If silicon is technically an insulator at absolute zero, why does it conduct electricity at room temperature — and can we actually count how many charge carriers are doing the job? It turns out we can, and the answer is a beautifully balanced story. <<FOCUS:valence-band>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_5:carrier_balance>> <<SECTION:Intrinsic Semiconductors|id=sec-1>>Picture the silicon crystal at room temperature. Every atom is vibrating. Most of the time, all bonding electrons stay put — but every so often, a vibrating atom gives one of those electrons just enough of a kick to break free. <<FOCUS:thermal-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Thermal energy → breaks covalent bond|id=text-1>>That freed electron shoots up into the conduction band, where it can wander and carry current. At the exact same moment, it leaves behind an empty spot in the bond — a hole — which acts like a positive charge carrier moving through the crystal. <<TRACE:thermal-arrow>> So for every free electron created, exactly one hole is created. They're born in pairs — electron-hole pairs. And this is happening constantly, all across the crystal. <<POINT:free-electron>> <<POINT:free-electron>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Free electron + hole = electron-hole pair|id=text-2>>But here's the question: does the crystal just keep filling up with more and more free electrons forever? <<POINT:conduction-band>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:recombination-arrow>> No — because the reverse process also happens. A free electron in the conduction band occasionally loses energy, drops back down, and fills a hole. The pair disappears. This is called recombination. <<TRACE:recombination-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Generation ⇌ Recombination → steady state|id=text-3>>Eventually, the rate of pair creation exactly balances the rate of recombination. A steady state is reached, and the number of electron-hole pairs settles at a nearly constant value. <<POINT:carrier-count-label>> <<FOCUS:carrier-count-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Silicon at 300 K: n ≈ p ≈ 7 × 10¹⁵ per cubic metre|id=key-1>>For silicon at room temperature — that's three hundred kelvin — this steady-state density is about seven times ten to the power fifteen electron-hole pairs per cubic metre. That's seven quadrillion per cubic metre. A staggeringly large number, yet still tiny compared to a metal. <<PAUSE:short>> For silicon at three hundred kelvin, the density of free electrons and holes are equal and settle at approximately seven times ten to the power fifteen per cubic metre. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n = p \approx 7 \times 10^{15} \, \text{m}^{-3}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:doping|to=0.7|duration=1800>> Now watch what happens when we add impurities — doping. Say we add a phosphorus atom, which has five outer electrons instead of four. Four of them form bonds with silicon neighbours, but the fifth is nearly free. <<FOCUS:free-electron>> <<WRITE_TEXT:n-type: extra electrons from donor atoms|id=text-4>>Those donor electrons jump easily into the conduction band. So suddenly we have many more free electrons — the electron density n shoots up dramatically. Here's an example from the chapter — Example forty-five point two. We have an n-type semiconductor, and we're asked to find its resistivity given some carrier data. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the resistivity of an n-type semiconductor given: nₑ = 8×10¹³ cm⁻³, nₕ = 5×10¹² cm⁻³, μₑ = 2.3×10⁴ cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹, μₕ = 100 cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹|id=ex-q-1>> The density of conduction electrons is eight times ten to the thirteen per cubic centimeter, which converts to eight times ten to the nineteen per cubic meter. The density of holes is five times ten to the twelve per cubic centimeter, converting to five times ten to the eighteen per cubic meter. The mobility of conduction electrons is two point three times ten to the four square centimeters per volt per second, which is two point three square meters per volt per second in SI units. And the mobility of holes is one hundred square centimeters per volt per second, which converts to ten to the negative two square meters per volt per second. When you dope a semiconductor, increasing one type of carrier forces the other type down — their product stays fixed for a given material at a given temperature. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n \times p = \text{constant}|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start by writing the conductivity formula. For a semiconductor with both conduction electrons and holes, sigma equals e times the quantity n-e times mu-e plus n-h times mu-h. <<WRITE_STEP:σ = e(nₑμₑ + nₕμₕ)|id=ex-step-1-1>> The charge of the electron e is one point six times ten to the negative nineteen coulombs. Now let's plug in all our SI values. <<WRITE_STEP:σ = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) × [(8 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³)(2.3 m² V⁻¹s⁻¹) + (5 × 10¹⁸ m⁻³)(10⁻² m² V⁻¹s⁻¹)]|id=ex-step-1-2>> Let's evaluate what's inside the brackets first. The electron contribution is eight times ten to the nineteen multiplied by two point three, which gives eighteen point four times ten to the nineteen. The hole contribution is five times ten to the eighteen multiplied by ten to the negative two, giving five times ten to the sixteen. That second term is much smaller, so the electron term dominates — this makes sense for an n-type semiconductor. Adding them together and multiplying by one point six times ten to the negative nineteen gives us a conductivity of approximately two point nine four coulombs per meter per volt per second. <<WRITE_STEP:σ ≈ 2.94 C m⁻¹ V⁻¹ s⁻¹|id=ex-step-1-3>> Finally, the resistivity rho equals one divided by sigma. <<WRITE_STEP:ρ = 1/σ|id=ex-step-1-4>> So we divide one by two point nine four to get the resistivity. <<PAUSE:short>> And the answer is approximately zero point three four ohm meters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ρ = 1/2.94 ≈ 0.34 Ω·m|id=ex-ans-1>> But here's the crucial twist: with so many extra electrons around, any hole that forms gets filled almost instantly. The hole density p plummets. The product n times p stays constant. <<POINT:np-product-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:np-product-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:n × p = constant for a given semiconductor|id=key-2>>This is the law of mass action for semiconductors. Boost the electrons with doping, and holes become rare. Boost the holes with p-type doping, and electrons become rare. The product never changes — it's fixed by the material and the temperature. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Heat up a metal wire and it resists more — that makes sense, right? Now heat up a semiconductor and something completely backwards happens: it actually gets BETTER at conducting. How can heat make something less resistive? <<FOCUS:band-gap-arrow>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:2_94 m:semiconductor_temp>> <<SECTION:Semiconductors vs Metals — Temperature Effect|id=sec-1>>To understand this, picture the energy landscape inside a semiconductor. Electrons sit in the valence band — a low-energy zone — and they'd love to jump up into the conduction band where they can move freely. But there's a gap in between, the band gap. <<FOCUS:electron-low-temp>> At low temperatures, almost no electrons have enough energy to leap that gap. So we have very few free carriers — barely any current can flow. Here's the key question: what changes when we crank up the temperature? <<POINT:electron-low-temp>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:temperature|to=90.0|from=10.0|duration=2500>> <<WRITE_KEY:More heat → more electron-hole pairs → lower resistivity|id=key-1>>Watch what happens as temperature rises — electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the gap. Every electron that jumps up leaves behind a hole in the valence band. We get electron-hole PAIRS, and the count of these pairs grows rapidly with temperature. <<PAUSE:short>> The number of electron-hole pairs grows with temperature in a very specific way — it scales with temperature to the power of three halves, multiplied by an exponential that depends on the band gap divided by the thermal energy. A bigger band gap means fewer pairs; a higher temperature means exponentially more. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n_{pairs} \propto T^{3/2}\, e^{-\Delta E / 2kT}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:electron-high-temp>> <<WRITE_TEXT:More carriers → conductivity up, resistivity DOWN|id=text-1>>Yes, thermal collisions do slow each carrier a little — just like in a metal. But that effect is tiny compared to the explosion in the NUMBER of carriers. So the net result: resistivity falls as temperature rises. The temperature coefficient is NEGATIVE for semiconductors — roughly negative zero point zero seven per kelvin for silicon. A metal does the exact opposite. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:p-region>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:2_94 m:pn_junction>> <<SECTION:The p-n Junction|id=sec-2>>Now let's talk about what happens when we join two types of semiconductor side by side. On the left, p-type material — doped so it has an abundance of holes, positive charge carriers. On the right, n-type — doped so it has an abundance of free electrons. <<FOCUS:depletion-zone>> The moment these two sides touch, electrons from the n-side diffuse over and fill holes on the p-side. This creates a narrow zone right at the junction where all the carriers have cancelled out. We call it the depletion region. <<FOCUS:built-in-field-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Depletion region → built-in E field (n to p)|id=text-2>>Because electrons left the n-side, that side becomes positively charged. Because electrons arrived on the p-side, it becomes negatively charged. This sets up a built-in electric field pointing from n to p — it acts like an invisible wall that stops MORE carriers from crossing. So here's the big question: can we push current through a p-n junction, and does it matter which way we push? <<POINT:depletion-zone>> <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a p-n junction diode, and we need to find its approximate dynamic resistance at two different forward bias voltages. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the dynamic resistance of a p-n junction at (a) forward bias of one volt, and (b) forward bias of two volts.|id=ex-q-1>> Remember, dynamic resistance is defined as R equals delta V divided by delta i — that is, a small change in voltage divided by the corresponding small change in current. Let's tackle part a first. At a forward bias of one volt, the current through the diode is ten milliamperes. Now we look at a nearby point on the characteristic curve: at one point two volts, the current is fifteen milliamperes. So the change in voltage is zero point two volts, and the change in current is five milliamperes. <<WRITE_STEP:(a) At V = 1 V, i = 10 mA; at V = 1.2 V, i = 15 mA|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:ΔV = 0.2 V, Δi = 5 mA|id=ex-step-1-2>> Plugging into the formula, R equals delta V divided by delta i equals zero point two volts divided by five milliamperes. <<WRITE_STEP:R = ΔV / Δi = 0.2 V / 5 mA = 40 Ω|id=ex-step-1-3>> That gives us a dynamic resistance of forty ohms at one volt forward bias. Notice this is quite a significant resistance — we're still in the lower region of the forward bias curve where the diode hasn't fully turned on. Now for part b, at a higher forward bias of two volts, the current has jumped dramatically to four hundred milliamperes. At two point one volts, the current is eight hundred milliamperes. So the change in voltage is zero point one volts, and the change in current is four hundred milliamperes — a huge swing for a tiny voltage step! <<WRITE_STEP:(b) At V = 2 V, i = 400 mA; at V = 2.1 V, i = 800 mA|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:ΔV = 0.1 V, Δi = 400 mA|id=ex-step-1-5>> Applying the formula again, R equals zero point one volts divided by four hundred milliamperes. <<WRITE_STEP:R = ΔV / Δi = 0.1 V / 400 mA = 0.25 Ω|id=ex-step-1-6>> That gives us just zero point two five ohms — a tiny fraction of what we got in part a. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:(a) Dynamic resistance at 1 V forward bias = 40 Ω  |  (b) Dynamic resistance at 2 V forward bias = 0.25 Ω|id=ex-ans-1>> And this beautifully illustrates the key lesson: as forward bias increases and the diode conducts more heavily, the dynamic resistance drops dramatically — from forty ohms all the way down to zero point two five ohms — because the curve gets much steeper and a small voltage change produces a very large change in current. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Given a mobility value of two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb to the power of negative one, find the resulting resistivity.|id=ex-q-1>> We're given a mobility — that's the drift speed per unit electric field per unit charge — of two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb, raised to the negative one power. Our job is to figure out the resistivity that comes from that value. Now, resistivity is inversely related to the mobility. So we take the reciprocal of our mobility value. <<WRITE_STEP:rho = 1 / (2.94 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ C⁻¹)|id=ex-step-1-1>> In other words, we flip the two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb quantity to get our resistivity. Carrying out that division gives us our result. <<WRITE_ANSWER:rho ≈ 0.34 ohm-meters|id=ex-ans-1>> The resulting resistivity is approximately zero point three four ohm-meters. So a mobility of two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb to the negative one gives a resistivity of about zero point three four ohm-meters. Here's an example from the chapter. We're looking at silicon, a semiconductor material, and we want to identify its temperature coefficient of resistivity. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the average temperature coefficient of resistivity for silicon?|id=ex-q-1>> Recall that for metals the temperature coefficient of resistivity is positive — meaning resistivity goes up with temperature. But silicon is a semiconductor, and semiconductors behave differently. As temperature rises, more charge carriers become available, so resistivity actually decreases. This means the coefficient must be negative. <<WRITE_STEP:Silicon is a semiconductor → resistivity decreases as temperature increases|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Therefore: temperature coefficient of resistivity α < 0|id=ex-step-1-2>> And indeed, the textbook confirms this. The average value of the temperature coefficient of resistivity for silicon is negative zero point zero seven per kelvin. <<PAUSE:short>> That negative sign is the key result — it tells us definitively that silicon's resistivity goes down as temperature goes up, which is the hallmark of a semiconductor. <<WRITE_ANSWER:α (silicon) = negative zero point zero seven per kelvin|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on p-n junction rectifier circuits. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In a rectifier circuit, the p-n junction is forward biased. And so the current through the load is simply the source voltage divided by R. <<PAUSE:short>> Using Ohm's law, i is approximately V zero divided by R, times sine of omega t plus phi. <<WRITE_ANSWER:i ≈ V zero divided by R, times sine of omega t plus phi|id=ex-ans-3>> That is the answer — because junction resistance is negligible compared to R, the full source voltage effectively appears across the load, and the current follows that same sinusoidal shape, scaled by one over R. Here's an example from the chapter on LEDs and visible light. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Under what conditions does an LED emit visible light, and which semiconductor materials can produce it?|id=ex-q-1>> When an electron and a hole recombine inside an LED, they release energy as a photon. The key question is: does that photon's wavelength fall inside the visible range? The textbook tells us the visible range runs from three hundred eighty nanometers all the way up to seven hundred eighty nanometers — anything outside that window, and our eyes simply cannot see it. Now, not every semiconductor hits that window. <<WRITE_STEP:Silicon and germanium → photon wavelengths in the infrared (beyond 780 nm) → NOT visible|id=ex-step-1-1>> Silicon and germanium are the workhorses of electronics, but the photon wavelengths they produce by electron-hole recombination fall in the infrared range — beyond seven hundred eighty nanometers. So even though they are emitting photons, those photons are invisible to us. A silicon or germanium LED is not a useful light source for anything we can see with our eyes. To get visible light, we need materials whose recombination energy lands a photon between three hundred eighty and seven hundred eighty nanometers. <<WRITE_STEP:Compound semiconductors, e.g. gallium arsenide, indium phosphide → photon wavelengths inside 380 nm – 780 nm → visible light emitted|id=ex-step-1-2>> Compounds like gallium arsenide and indium phosphide have the right bandgap energies to do exactly that. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Visible LEDs require photon wavelength in 380 nm – 780 nm; achievable with compounds such as gallium arsenide or indium phosphide — NOT with silicon or germanium (infrared)|id=ex-ans-1>> So the answer is: an LED glows visibly only when its semiconductor material produces photons in the three-hundred-eighty to seven-hundred-eighty nanometer range, and that rules out silicon and germanium entirely — you need compound materials like gallium arsenide or indium phosphide to build a working visible-light LED. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:forward-bias-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:p-n junction = one-way gate; forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks|id=key-2>>Absolutely — direction is everything. Forward bias: connect positive to the p-side and negative to the n-side, and your external voltage OPPOSES the built-in field. The depletion region shrinks, the barrier falls, and current flows freely. Reverse bias: flip it, the depletion region WIDENS, the barrier grows, and almost no current gets through. The junction is a one-way gate. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So to wrap it up — semiconductors are fascinating precisely because they BREAK the rules we learned for metals. Heat them up and they conduct better, because more carriers are born. Join p-type to n-type and you get a junction that only lets current pass one way — and that's the foundation of every diode, every transistor, every chip in your phone. <<PAUSE:short>>

What if you could control a flood of water with just a tiny trickle — use a few drops to turn a river on or off? That is literally what a transistor does, but with electrons. And right now, there are more transistors on Earth than there are grains of sand on every beach. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_9:transistor_structure>> <<SECTION:The Sandwich Structure|id=sec-1>>A transistor is a semiconductor sandwich. Take two slices of n-type material and press an incredibly thin slice of p-type in between — about one micrometer thick, thinner than a human hair divided into one hundred pieces. That gives you an n-p-n transistor. <<TRACE:base-region>> <<FOCUS:emitter-region>> <<WRITE_TEXT:n-p-n: emitter (n, heavy) | base (p, thin, light) | collector (n, moderate)|id=text-1>>The three layers each have a name. The heavily doped outer layer that launches the electrons is the emitter. The thin lightly doped middle layer is the base. The moderately doped outer layer that gathers the electrons is the collector. Three layers, three terminals. <<FOCUS:eb-junction>> So here is the crucial question: how do you actually make this sandwich do something useful? How do you connect a battery to it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:eb-junction>> <<SECTION:Biasing — the golden rule|id=sec-2>>Here is the golden rule of transistor operation: you always forward-bias the emitter–base junction, and you always reverse-bias the collector–base junction. Forward bias on the left, reverse bias on the right — every single time. <<POINT:eb-junction>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:eb-junction>> <<WRITE_KEY:EB junction: forward biased | CB junction: reverse biased|id=key-1>>Forward bias on the emitter–base junction lowers the barrier, so conduction electrons from the emitter are pushed hard into the thin base region. That part makes sense — it is just like a normal forward-biased p-n junction. <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is where the magic happens. Those electrons arrive in the base. The base is p-type, so some electrons do recombine with holes there — but the base is so incredibly thin and so lightly doped that most electrons do NOT recombine. They drift straight across and slam into the reverse-biased collector junction. <<TRACE:electron-flow-arrow>> <<FOCUS:collector-region>> And the reverse-biased collector junction actually helps — its electric field sweeps those electrons right into the collector. So the vast majority of electrons flow emitter to collector. Only a tiny fraction escape out through the base terminal. <<POINT:collector-region>> All the current that enters the emitter must split between the tiny base current and the large collector current — charge is conserved, so emitter current equals base current plus collector current. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I_E = I_B + I_C|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:I_E = I_B + I_C|id=step-1>>All the current entering the emitter must go somewhere — charge is conserved. So emitter current equals base current plus collector current. The base current is tiny; the collector current is large. Emitter current is I sub E, base current is I sub B, collector current is I sub C. <<POINT:ib-label>> <<POINT:ib-label>> <<FOCUS:base-terminal>> So ask yourself — if a tiny base current controls whether most electrons make it to the collector, what happens if you increase the base current just a little? <<PAUSE:long>> The ratio of the collector current to the base current is what we call the current gain, beta. It tells you how many times larger the collector current is compared to the tiny base current that controls it. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example straight from the chapter on junction transistors. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Given that IB is about one to five percent of IE, find the typical ranges of alpha and beta for a transistor.|id=ex-q-1>> The key relationship is that the base current is very small compared to the emitter current — only one to five percent of it. This is what makes transistors so special. Let's work out alpha first. Alpha equals I C divided by I E — that is, the collector current over the emitter current. <<WRITE_STEP:alpha = IC / IE|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, since I B is one to five percent of I E, that means I C makes up the remaining ninety-five to ninety-nine percent of I E. <<WRITE_STEP:IC = IE − IB ≈ 0.95 × IE  to  0.99 × IE|id=ex-step-1-2>> So alpha comes out to approximately zero point nine five to zero point nine nine — very close to one. Now for beta. Beta equals I C divided by I B — collector current over base current. <<WRITE_STEP:beta = IC / IB|id=ex-step-1-3>> Because I B is only one to five percent of I E, and I C is nearly all of I E, the ratio I C over I B is enormous. <<WRITE_STEP:beta = IC / IB ≈ IE / (0.01 to 0.05) × IE  →  beta ≈ 20 to 100|id=ex-step-1-4>> A tiny base current controls a collector current that is twenty to one hundred times larger — that is exactly how a transistor amplifies. <<PAUSE:short>> And so the answer is: <<WRITE_ANSWER:alpha ≈ 0.95 to 0.99  |  beta ≈ 20 to 100|id=ex-ans-1>> Alpha is approximately zero point nine five to zero point nine nine, and beta is approximately twenty to one hundred. Because the base current is only one to five percent of the emitter current, alpha is close to one and beta is much greater than one — which is why transistors amplify so effectively. Here's an example from the chapter on junction transistors. We want to show that the current gain beta is not independent of alpha — they're linked by a single relation that comes straight from Kirchhoff's current law. The setup facts are: at any transistor junction, the emitter current I E equals the base current I B plus the collector current I C. We also define alpha as I C divided by I E, and beta as I C divided by I B. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Show that beta = alpha divided by (1 minus alpha), using Kirchhoff's current law IE = IB + IC.|id=ex-q-1>> We start from Kirchhoff's current law: I E equals I B plus I C. To connect this to alpha and beta, we divide every term throughout by I C. <<WRITE_STEP:Start: IE = IB + IC|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Divide throughout by IC: IE/IC = IB/IC + 1|id=ex-step-1-2>> Dividing I E by I C gives one over alpha, and dividing I B by I C gives one over beta, so the equation becomes one over alpha equals one over beta plus one. Now let's write that substitution explicitly. Since alpha equals I C divided by I E, we have I E divided by I C equals one over alpha. And since beta equals I C divided by I B, we have I B divided by I C equals one over beta. Substituting both in: <<WRITE_STEP:1/alpha = 1/beta + 1|id=ex-step-1-3>> Now we rearrange to isolate one over beta. Subtracting one from both sides gives one over beta equals one over alpha minus one, which we can write as one minus alpha all over alpha. <<WRITE_STEP:1/beta = 1/alpha − 1 = (1 − alpha)/alpha|id=ex-step-1-4>> Taking the reciprocal of both sides then gives us beta directly. Taking reciprocals of both sides, we arrive at the final result. <<PAUSE:short>> Beta equals alpha divided by one minus alpha. <<WRITE_ANSWER:beta = alpha / (1 − alpha)|id=ex-ans-1>> This is the key relationship: alpha and beta are not independent — once you know one, Kirchhoff's current law completely determines the other. Here's an example from the chapter on junction transistors. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A transistor amplifier has a load resistance R L in the collector circuit. The current gain is defined as delta I C divided by delta I B, and is typically of the order of fifty. What is the change in output voltage across R L?|id=ex-q-1>> The key quantities are: the current gain — that's the ratio of the change in collector current to the change in base current — is typically around fifty, and the change in output voltage delta V equals R L times delta I C, where R L is the load resistance in the collector circuit. We start by writing down the two core relationships. <<WRITE_STEP:Current gain = delta I C / delta I B ≈ 50|id=ex-step-1-1>> The current gain tells us how much the collector current changes for every unit change in base current — a small wiggle in the base current gets amplified by a factor of around fifty at the collector. <<WRITE_STEP:Change in output voltage: delta V = R L × delta I C|id=ex-step-1-2>> So whatever change in collector current that amplification produces, we multiply it by the load resistance R L to get the change in the voltage across that resistor in the collector circuit. And that's the answer. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta V = R L × delta I C, with current gain delta I C / delta I B of order fifty|id=ex-ans-1>> The change in output voltage is simply the load resistance multiplied by the change in collector current. Because the current gain is typically of the order of fifty, even a tiny change in the base current produces a collector current change fifty times as large, and the full voltage swing across R L reflects that amplification. Here's an example from the chapter on junction transistors. We have a common-emitter transistor amplifier with an input signal voltage v i applied to the base. The dynamic resistance of the forward-biased base-emitter junction — also called the input resistance — is R B E. The load resistance in the collector circuit is R L, and beta is the current amplification factor, which is of the order of fifty. We want to find the voltage gain, current gain, and power gain of this amplifier. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the voltage gain, current gain, and power gain of a common-emitter amplifier in terms of beta, RL, and RBE.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the base circuit. The input signal voltage v i is applied across the base-emitter junction whose resistance is R B E. So by Ohm's law, the change in base current delta I B equals v i divided by R B E. <<WRITE_STEP:ΔI_B = v_i / R_{BE}|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, the collector current I C is related to the base current I B through the transistor's current gain: I C equals beta times I B. So when the base current changes by delta I B, the resulting change in collector current delta I C equals beta times delta I B, which substituting gives us beta times v i divided by R B E. <<WRITE_STEP:ΔI_C = β · ΔI_B = β · v_i / R_{BE}|id=ex-step-1-2>> Next, this change in collector current flows through the load resistance R L, so the output voltage v o — that is, the change in voltage across R L — equals R L times delta I C. Substituting our expression for delta I C, we get v o equals beta times v i times R L divided by R B E. <<WRITE_STEP:v_o = R_L · ΔI_C = β · v_i · R_L / R_{BE}|id=ex-step-1-3>> Now we can read off the voltage gain directly: it is v o divided by v i, which equals beta times R L divided by R B E. <<WRITE_STEP:Voltage Gain = v_o / v_i = β · R_L / R_{BE}|id=ex-step-1-4>> Since beta is of the order of fifty and R L may be much larger than R B E, the voltage gain is high. Now for the current gain. That's simply the ratio of the change in collector current delta I C to the change in base current delta I B. We already know delta I C equals beta times delta I B, so dividing through, the current gain equals beta. <<WRITE_STEP:Current Gain = ΔI_C / ΔI_B = β|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<PAUSE:short>> And finally, power gain equals voltage gain times current gain. Substituting, that's beta times R L over R B E, multiplied by beta, giving us beta squared times R L divided by R B E. <<WRITE_STEP:Power Gain = Voltage Gain × Current Gain = β² · R_L / R_{BE}|id=ex-step-1-6>> So to summarise the three gains for a common-emitter amplifier: the voltage gain is beta times R L divided by R B E, the current gain is simply beta, and the power gain is beta squared times R L divided by R B E. Since beta is of the order of fifty, the power gain is enormous — of the order of two thousand five hundred times R L over R B E. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Voltage Gain = β·RL/RBE | Current Gain = β | Power Gain = β²·RL/RBE|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on junction transistors. We have a transistor oscillator circuit that includes an L C network — that is, a network made up of an inductor with inductance L and a capacitor with capacitance C. The question is: at what frequency does this network resonate, and how can that frequency be tuned? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: An LC network in a transistor oscillator has inductance L and capacitance C. Find the resonant frequency, and state how it can be varied.|id=ex-q-1>> The resonant frequency of an L C network is given by the standard formula: omega zero equals one divided by two pi times the square root of L times C. Here, L is the inductance of the inductor in the L C network, and C is the capacitance of the capacitor in the L C network. <<WRITE_STEP:omega_0 = 1 / (2π √(LC))|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:where L = inductance of the inductor, C = capacitance of the capacitor|indent=1|id=ex-step-1-2>> This is the frequency at which the circuit naturally oscillates, and it becomes the output frequency of the transistor oscillator. And that's the answer. <<PAUSE:short>> The L C network resonates at omega zero equals one divided by two pi times the square root of L times C. Crucially, this frequency can be varied by varying either L or C — increase the inductance or the capacitance and the frequency drops; decrease either one and the frequency rises. That's how oscillator circuits are tuned in practice. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Resonant frequency: omega_0 = 1 / (2π √(LC)). Frequency can be varied by varying L or C.|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ic-label>> <<WRITE_STEP:beta = I_C divided by I_B|id=step-2>>The collector current goes up by a lot! The ratio of collector current to base current is called the current gain, beta. A typical transistor has a beta of fifty to three hundred — meaning one milliamp of base current can control over one hundred milliamps at the collector. A tiny signal controls a huge one. That is amplification. <<POINT:ic-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:electron-flow-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Small I_B controls large I_C — current gain beta = I_C / I_B|id=key-2>>To summarise: a transistor works because the emitter–base junction is forward-biased, pushing a flood of electrons into the ultra-thin base, and the reverse-biased collector–base junction sweeps almost all of them into the collector. The base current is the tiny tap that controls the river. <<TRACE:electron-flow-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>
