Every computer on the planet — every phone, every calculator, every game console — is built from billions of tiny decision-makers that can only ever say two things: zero or one. How on earth does that tiny yes-or-no world produce something as rich as the internet? <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:The Binary World|id=sec-1>><<WRITE_TEXT:0 = off / false / open, 1 = on / true / closed|id=text-1>>Let's agree on the rules of this tiny world. Zero means off, open, false — anything that isn't happening. One means on, closed, true — anything that is happening. We call these logical variables, and every signal in a digital circuit is always exactly one of these two. Now here is the big question: if we have two switches, can we combine them to make decisions? Let's find out with a simple light-bulb experiment. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:switches-series-analogy>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_10:logic_gates_diagram>> <<SECTION:AND Gate|id=sec-2>><<WRITE_TEXT:AND: output is 1 only when BOTH inputs are 1|id=text-2>>Look at this circuit — two switches in series. The bulb only lights up when switch one AND switch two are both closed. If either one is open, no current flows, bulb stays off. <<FOCUS:and-gate-symbol>> We give this rule a name: the AND gate. Here is its symbol — two inputs A and B go in, one output C comes out. C is one if and only if A is one AND B is one. Every other combination gives zero. <<POINT:and-gate-symbol>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:and-truth-table>> <<WRITE_TEXT:AND truth table: 1,1 → 1 only|id=text-3>>We can write all four possible input combinations in a truth table. Zero-zero gives zero. Zero-one gives zero. One-zero gives zero. Only one-one gives one. The AND gate is a strict gate — it demands everything. <<POINT:and-truth-table>> <<FOCUS:switches-parallel-analogy>> <<SECTION:OR Gate|id=sec-3>><<WRITE_TEXT:OR: output is 1 when ANY input is 1|id=text-4>>Now let's wire the two switches in parallel instead. Either switch closed completes the circuit. The bulb lights up if switch one OR switch two — or both — are closed. <<FOCUS:or-gate-symbol>> This is the OR gate. C is one if A is one, or B is one, or both are one. The only time the output is zero is when both inputs are zero — the gate is generous, it accepts any positive signal. <<POINT:or-gate-symbol>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:or-truth-table>> <<WRITE_TEXT:OR truth table: 0,0 → 0 only|id=text-5>>The truth table confirms it: zero-zero gives zero, but zero-one, one-zero, and one-one all give one. Compare that with AND — the OR gate is far more permissive. <<POINT:or-truth-table>> <<FOCUS:not-gate-symbol>> <<SECTION:NOT Gate|id=sec-4>><<WRITE_TEXT:NOT: output is the opposite of input|id=text-6>>The third gate is the simplest of all — the NOT gate. It has just one input and it simply flips it. If A is zero, the output is one. If A is one, the output is zero. It is a perfect inverter. <<FOCUS:not-truth-table>> <<WRITE_TEXT:NOT truth table: 0→1, 1→0|id=text-7>>The truth table for NOT is just two rows: zero becomes one, one becomes zero. Notice the little bubble on the output of the gate symbol — that bubble always means inversion in electronics. <<POINT:not-truth-table>> Here's an example from the chapter. We need to write the truth table for the logical function Z equals X AND Y, all of that OR X. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the truth table for Z = (X AND Y) OR X|id=ex-q-1>> We have two independent variables: X and Y. To keep things manageable, we introduce an intermediate variable — let's call it W — where W equals X AND Y. Then Z equals W OR X. We'll build the truth table column by column. Let's lay out all four combinations of X and Y, and work out W equals X AND Y for each row. Remember, W is one only when both X and Y are one — that's the AND rule. <<WRITE_STEP:X | Y | W = X AND Y | Z = W OR X|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:0 | 0 |      0      |     ?|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:0 | 1 |      0      |     ?|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:1 | 0 |      0      |     ?|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:1 | 1 |      1      |     ?|id=ex-step-1-5>> So W is zero in the first three rows, and one only in the last row where both X and Y are one. Now we evaluate Z equals W OR X for each row. In the first row, X is zero and Y is zero, so W is zero and X is zero — W OR X gives zero, so Z is zero. In the second row, X is zero and Y is one, so W is still zero and X is zero — W OR X is again zero, so Z is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:Row 1: X=0, Y=0 → W=0, Z = 0 OR 0 = 0|id=ex-step-1-6>> <<WRITE_STEP:Row 2: X=0, Y=1 → W=0, Z = 0 OR 0 = 0|id=ex-step-1-7>> Continuing — in the third row, X is one and Y is zero, so W is zero but X is one. W OR X equals zero OR one, which is one, so Z is one. In the fourth row, X is one and Y is one, so W is one and X is one. W OR X equals one OR one, which is one, so Z is one. <<WRITE_STEP:Row 3: X=1, Y=0 → W=0, Z = 0 OR 1 = 1|id=ex-step-1-8>> <<WRITE_STEP:Row 4: X=1, Y=1 → W=1, Z = 1 OR 1 = 1|id=ex-step-1-9>> Putting it all together, here is the complete truth table. <<PAUSE:short>> The final answer is: when X is zero and Y is zero, Z is zero; when X is zero and Y is one, Z is zero; when X is one and Y is zero, Z is one; and when X is one and Y is one, Z is one. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Truth Table for Z = (X AND Y) OR X:
X=0, Y=0 → Z=0
X=0, Y=1 → Z=0
X=1, Y=0 → Z=1
X=1, Y=1 → Z=1|id=ex-ans-1>> Notice that Z turns on whenever X is one, regardless of Y — which also matches the simplified form: Z equals X AND Y, all of that OR X. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Construct the truth table for X of A and B, where an OR gate and an AND gate are combined as shown.|id=ex-q-1>> The circuit uses one OR gate and one AND gate. The OR gate takes A and B as its inputs, and its output is Y equals A OR B. The AND gate then takes A and Y as its inputs, giving a final output X equals A AND open-bracket A OR B close-bracket. Our job is to build the complete truth table by working through every combination of A and B. We start by introducing the intermediate variable Y. Since the OR gate takes A and B, we write Y equals A OR B. <<WRITE_STEP:Y = A OR B  (output of the OR gate)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Then the AND gate receives A and Y, so the final output is X equals A AND open-bracket A OR B close-bracket. <<WRITE_STEP:X = A AND (A OR B)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now let's set up the table with columns for A, B, Y, and X. <<WRITE_STEP:A | B | Y = A OR B | X = A AND (A OR B)|id=ex-step-1-3>> Let's fill in the first two rows. When A is zero and B is zero, the OR gate sees two zeros, so Y is zero. The AND gate then has A equals zero and Y equals zero, giving X equals zero. <<WRITE_STEP:A=0, B=0 → Y = 0 OR 0 = 0,  X = 0 AND 0 = 0|id=ex-step-1-4>> Next, when A is zero and B is one, the OR gate gives Y equals one. But the AND gate has A equals zero, so X equals zero AND one, which is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:A=0, B=1 → Y = 0 OR 1 = 1,  X = 0 AND 1 = 0|id=ex-step-1-5>> Now the last two rows. When A is one and B is zero, the OR gate gives Y equals one OR zero, which is one. The AND gate gets A equals one and Y equals one, so X equals one AND one, which is one. <<WRITE_STEP:A=1, B=0 → Y = 1 OR 0 = 1,  X = 1 AND 1 = 1|id=ex-step-1-6>> Finally, when A is one and B is one, the OR gate gives Y equals one. The AND gate gets A equals one and Y equals one, so X equals one again. <<WRITE_STEP:A=1, B=1 → Y = 1 OR 1 = 1,  X = 1 AND 1 = 1|id=ex-step-1-7>> Putting it all together, the complete truth table is: <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:A=0, B=0 → Y=0, X=0 | A=0, B=1 → Y=1, X=0 | A=1, B=0 → Y=1, X=1 | A=1, B=1 → Y=1, X=1|id=ex-ans-1>> Notice that X equals one only when A is one, regardless of B. The OR gate's output Y ensures the AND gate always has a one on one input whenever A is one, so X simply follows A. The key technique here was naming the intermediate output Y first, then evaluating the final gate — step by step. Here's an example from the chapter. We have two input variables, A and B. Each input is first inverted by a NOT gate — so A becomes NOT A, and B becomes NOT B. Then those two inverted signals are fed into a NAND gate. The question is: what does the overall output look like across all four possible input combinations? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Two NOT gates feeding A and B, then a NAND gate — does the output equal A OR B?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's build the truth table step by step to find out. We set up the truth table with columns for A, B, NOT A, NOT B, and the final NAND output. The NAND gate takes NOT A and NOT B as its inputs, so the output is NOT of open-bracket NOT A AND NOT B close-bracket. Let's write the column headers first. <<WRITE_STEP:Columns: A | B | NOT A | NOT B | NOT(NOT A AND NOT B)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we fill in the NOT A and NOT B columns — they simply flip each bit. When A is zero, NOT A is one; when A is one, NOT A is zero. Same rule for B. Let's go through each of the four rows. Row one: A is zero, B is zero. NOT A is one, NOT B is one. NOT A AND NOT B is one, so the NAND output — which is NOT of that — is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:A=0, B=0 → NOT A=1, NOT B=1 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=1 → Output = 0|id=ex-step-1-2>> Row two: A is zero, B is one. NOT A is one, NOT B is zero. NOT A AND NOT B is zero, so the NAND output is one. <<WRITE_STEP:A=0, B=1 → NOT A=1, NOT B=0 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=0 → Output = 1|id=ex-step-1-3>> Row three: A is one, B is zero. NOT A is zero, NOT B is one. NOT A AND NOT B is zero, NAND output is one. <<WRITE_STEP:A=1, B=0 → NOT A=0, NOT B=1 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=0 → Output = 1|id=ex-step-1-4>> Row four: A is one, B is one. NOT A is zero, NOT B is zero. NOT A AND NOT B is zero, NAND output is one. <<WRITE_STEP:A=1, B=1 → NOT A=0, NOT B=0 → (NOT A AND NOT B)=0 → Output = 1|id=ex-step-1-5>> Now look at what we've got. The output is one whenever either A or B is one, or when both are one. The output is zero only when both A and B are zero — that is the one and only case where we get a zero. <<WRITE_STEP:Output is 0 only when both A = 0 and B = 0; output is 1 for all other combinations.|id=ex-step-1-6>> That pattern is exactly the definition of an OR gate. So this combination of two NOT gates followed by a NAND gate is completely equivalent to A OR B for all four input combinations. <<WRITE_ANSWER:NOT(NOT A AND NOT B) = A OR B  — the circuit behaves as an OR gate|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on logic gates. We're adding two one-digit binary numbers, A and B. The result has two digits: a carry digit C and a sum digit S. Let's build the full truth table to see what happens in every case. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Add two one-digit binary numbers A and B. Find the carry digit C and sum digit S for all combinations.|id=ex-q-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> We have four possible combinations. Zero plus zero gives us zero carry and zero sum. Zero plus one gives us zero carry and one sum. One plus zero gives us zero carry and one sum. And one plus one — since one-zero in binary equals two in decimal — gives us one carry and zero sum. <<WRITE_STEP:A=0, B=0 → C=0, S=0|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:A=0, B=1 → C=0, S=1|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:A=1, B=0 → C=0, S=1|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:A=1, B=1 → C=1, S=0  (since 10 in binary = 2 in decimal)|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now let's look at the pattern in that table. Focus on the carry digit C first. C is one only when both A and B are one — that's exactly the AND operation. So the carry C equals A AND B. <<WRITE_STEP:Carry: C = A AND B|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now look at the sum digit S. S is one when A and B are different — one is zero and the other is one — and zero when they're the same. That's the exclusive-OR, or XOR, operation. And if we write XOR out in terms of AND, OR, and NOT, the sum S equals A AND NOT B, OR NOT A AND B. <<WRITE_STEP:Sum: S = A XOR B = (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B)|id=ex-step-1-6>> So the final answer is this: in binary addition of two single digits, the carry digit C is given by the AND function — C equals A AND B — and the sum digit S is given by the XOR function — S equals A AND NOT B, OR NOT A AND B. <<PAUSE:short>> This means just two logic gates are enough to build a one-bit binary adder. <<WRITE_ANSWER:C = A AND B  |  S = A XOR B = (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:AND needs ALL ones. OR needs ANY one. NOT flips the input.|id=key-1>>So let's press this in: AND needs ALL inputs to be one to output one. OR needs ANY input to be one. NOT just flips whatever it receives. Three rules. That's the entire vocabulary of logic. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Billions of these gates, combined, = every computer ever made.|id=key-2>>And here is the truly mind-bending payoff: these three simple gates, combined in vast networks of billions, are all it takes to build every processor, every memory chip, every artificial intelligence system on the planet. The power isn't in one gate — it's in the combination. <<PAUSE:short>>

small base current label indicating tiny I_B at the base terminal
large collector current label indicating large I_C at the collector terminal

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We begin by asking why some materials conduct electricity and others don't — and discover that the answer lies in quantum energy bands, not just 'free electrons'. From there we see how tiny impurities transform a semiconductor's behaviour, how joining two doped materials creates a one-way valve for current, and finally how stacking these junctions gives us the transistor and the logic gates that power every digital device on Earth.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: Your smartphone contains over ten billion transistors on a chip the size of your fingernail — how can a material that barely conducts electricity at all become the engine of the entire digital world?

coverage_checklist.description: Distinguish conductors, insulators, and semiconductors by resistivity and by the qualitative picture of electron availability.
Explain how discrete atomic energy levels broaden into valence and conduction bands when atoms form a solid, and define the band gap.
Show why silicon and germanium are semiconductors by citing their small band gaps (1.1 eV and 0.68 eV) and contrast with insulators and metals.
Explain intrinsic vs extrinsic (n-type and p-type) semiconductors, the role of donor and acceptor dopants, and the concepts of electrons and holes as charge carriers.
Describe how thermal energy generates electron-hole pairs, why carrier density increases with temperature, and why semiconductor resistance falls as temperature rises (opposite to metals).
Explain the p-n junction: depletion region formation, built-in potential, forward and reverse bias, and rectification — establishing the diode as a one-way current valve.
Describe the structure and operation of an n-p-n (or p-n-p) junction transistor, explaining how a small base current controls a large collector current and enabling amplification and switching.
Introduce binary logic (0/1, off/on), define AND, OR, and NOT gates with truth tables, and connect transistor switching action to the physical realisation of logic gates.

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We opened by marvelling at ten billion transistors on a fingernail-sized chip — and now we can trace exactly how that's possible. Semiconductors occupy a sweet spot: their band gap is small enough that thermal energy or deliberate doping can populate the conduction band with electrons or holes. Joining p-type and n-type material creates a p-n junction that rectifies current; stacking two such junctions into a transistor lets a whisper of base current command a roar of collector current. Chain those transistors together and you implement AND, OR, and NOT — the three primitive operations from which every calculation your phone has ever performed is ultimately built. The quantum physics of energy bands, it turns out, is the foundation of the entire digital world.

segments.narration_chapter: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's something strange: silicon, the material inside every smartphone and computer chip, conducts electricity better when you heat it up — but copper, the material in your wiring, conducts worse when you heat it. Same universe, opposite behaviour. Why? <<FOCUS:conductor-band>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_1:conductivity_spectrum>> <<SECTION:Conductors — a quick reminder|id=sec-1>>Let's start with what we know. In a conductor like copper, electrons are barely clinging to their atoms. They wander freely everywhere, like a crowd milling around in a huge open hall. <<FOCUS:copper-marker>> Apply an electric field inside that conductor, and all those free electrons feel a force and start drifting together. That drift of charge is electric current. <<WRITE_TEXT:j = sigma × E — more sigma, more current|id=text-1>>The conductivity sigma tells us how easily current flows — bigger sigma, better conductor. The current density — how much charge flows per unit area — is directly proportional to the electric field we apply. The constant of proportionality is conductivity, sigma. Bigger sigma means more current for the same push. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{j} = \sigma \vec{E}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now, what happens when we heat up copper? The atoms vibrate more violently, and the free electrons keep crashing into them. Each collision interrupts their drift. <<WRITE_TEXT:More heat → more collisions → lower drift speed → lower sigma|id=text-2>>So sigma falls, and resistivity — the resistance per unit length — goes up. <<POINT:temp-up-conductor-arrow>> <<FOCUS:insulator-band>> At the other extreme, insulators like rubber or glass have electrons that are tightly locked to their nuclei. No free electrons, almost no current — sigma is tiny, even with a strong electric field. <<WRITE_TEXT:Insulator: electrons locked, sigma ≈ zero|id=text-3>> Resistivity is just the flip side of conductivity. If conductivity tells you how easy it is to push current through, resistivity tells you how hard it is. One is the reciprocal of the other. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:semiconductor-band>> <<SECTION:Semiconductors — the middle ground|id=sec-2>>So where does silicon fit? Right in the middle. <<WRITE_TEXT:Semiconductor: some free electrons, sigma between conductor and insulator|id=text-4>>It has some free electrons — far fewer than copper — so it conducts a little, but nowhere near as well as a metal. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the big question: what happens when we heat up silicon? In copper, heating HURT conduction. So should silicon also get worse? <<POINT:silicon-marker>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Semiconductor: heating FREES more electrons → sigma RISES|id=key-1>>Actually, the opposite happens. In silicon, the electrons are weakly bound — not totally free, not totally locked. When you add heat, some of those weakly-bound electrons gain enough energy to break free. So the number of free electrons increases, and conductivity goes UP. <<POINT:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:temp-up-conductor-arrow>> Look at the spectrum: copper is way over on the right with enormous conductivity that falls with heat. Silicon sits in the middle with a conductivity that rises with heat. These two arrows point in opposite directions — that's the defining signature of a semiconductor. <<POINT:temp-up-conductor-arrow>> <<SECTION:Why this matters|id=sec-3>>This temperature-sensitive conductivity is not a bug — it's the feature. It means we can control how well silicon conducts by adding tiny amounts of other atoms, or by heating it, or by shining light on it. <<WRITE_KEY:Controllable conductivity = the foundation of all electronics|id=key-2>>That controllability is exactly what makes semiconductors the foundation of every transistor, diode, and chip ever built. <<TRACE:semiconductor-band>> <<PAUSE:short>> So the paradox we started with has a clean answer: copper gets worse when heated because more collisions slow the electrons that are already free. Silicon gets better when heated because heat frees more electrons in the first place. Same physics — energy and electrons — but a completely different starting point. <<POINT:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<POINT:temp-up-semiconductor-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Why can copper carry electricity but a diamond — also full of electrons — absolutely refuses? Both materials are packed with electrons. So what is the secret difference? The answer lives not in the electrons themselves, but in the energy they are ALLOWED to have. <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:isolated-level>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_2:band_formation>> <<SECTION:Electrons in an isolated atom|id=sec-1>>Let's start with a single sodium atom sitting alone in space. Its electrons can only have certain fixed energies — one-s, two-s, two-p, three-s, and so on. Think of these as rungs on a ladder: an electron MUST sit on a rung. It cannot float between rungs. <<WRITE_TEXT:Atomic levels = fixed rungs (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s…)|id=text-1>>Sodium has eleven electrons. The inner levels — one-s, two-s, two-p — are completely filled. The outermost level, three-s, holds only one electron even though it could hold two. Everything above three-s is empty. <<POINT:isolated-level>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:n_atoms|to=3.0|from=1.0|duration=1800>> <<FOCUS:split-levels-few>> <<SECTION:Levels split into bands|id=sec-2>>Now bring a second sodium atom close. Suddenly those two three-s electrons can sense each other. The Pauli exclusion principle says no two electrons can share the same quantum state — so the single three-s level is FORCED to split into two slightly different energies. <<ANIMATE_PARAM:n_atoms|to=50.0|from=3.0|duration=2500>> <<FOCUS:band-region>> <<WRITE_TEXT:N atoms → N split levels → energy band|id=text-2>>Keep adding atoms — three, ten, a billion. Each new atom forces the level to split once more. By the time you have N atoms forming a solid, that single sharp three-s rung has split into N levels so densely packed they blur into a continuous smear. We call that smear an ENERGY BAND. <<PAUSE:short>> The total width of an energy band grows with the number of atoms N and how strongly they interact — the more atoms, the broader the smear of allowed energies. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E_{\text{band}} \approx N \times \Delta E_{\text{split}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each atomic level → one energy band in a solid|id=key-1>>This is the key idea: every atomic energy level becomes an energy band when atoms crowd together. The width of the band tells you how strongly those atoms are interacting. <<POINT:band-region>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:band-gap-region>> Now notice the gap between the three-s band and the three-p band above it. No allowed energy levels exist there — electrons are FORBIDDEN from having those energies. We call this the band gap, and it turns out to be the single most important feature of any solid. <<FOCUS:filled-half-marker>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Band gap = forbidden energy range|id=text-3>>Above the gap sits the three-p band — in sodium, completely empty. Below the gap is the three-s band — in sodium, only HALF full, because each sodium atom contributed just one electron to fill half of the available two-N states. <<POINT:filled-half-marker>> <<FOCUS:band-region>> Here is the question that connects everything: if you apply a voltage, why can an electron in a half-filled band accelerate, but an electron in a completely filled band cannot? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Current flows → electrons must move to slightly higher energy|id=text-4>>To carry current, an electron needs to speed up — gain a tiny bit of energy. In a HALF-FILLED band, empty levels are right next door at almost the same energy. The electron just hops up a fraction. Easy. <<POINT:filled-half-marker>> <<FOCUS:band-gap-region>> But in a COMPLETELY FILLED band, every level is occupied. There is nowhere to go — the Pauli principle blocks every adjacent slot. To move at all, the electron would need to leap across the entire band gap into the empty band above. If that gap is large, almost no electron can make that jump. The solid is an insulator. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter — Example forty five point one. We have a copper block, and we know that the mean free path of conduction electrons in copper is about four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. The question asks: what electric field is needed to give, on average, one electron volt of energy to a conduction electron? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the electric field E that gives a conduction electron 1 eV of energy in copper. (Mean free path d = 4 × 10⁻⁸ m)|id=ex-q-1>> Let's set up the physics. We call the electric field E. The force on the electron in that field is e times E, where e is the electron's charge. Now, as the electron moves through a distance d, the work done on it is force times distance — that is, e times E times d. This work equals the energy transferred to the electron. <<WRITE_STEP:Force on electron = eE|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Work done over distance d = eEd  (= energy transferred)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Before each collision, the electron travels an average distance equal to the mean free path — four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. So the energy transferred in one free path is e times E times four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. We want this to equal one electron volt. <<WRITE_STEP:Energy transferred = eE × (4 × 10⁻⁸ m)|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Set equal to 1 eV:   eE(4 × 10⁻⁸ m) = 1 eV|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now we solve for E. The e on the left cancels with the electron volt on the right — one electron volt is just one e times one volt — so we get E equals one volt divided by four times ten to the power of negative eight meters. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 1 V ÷ (4 × 10⁻⁸ m)|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<PAUSE:short>> Let's do that division: one divided by four times ten to the negative eight is two point five times ten to the power of seven. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 2.5 × 10⁷ V/m|id=ex-step-1-6>> And there's our answer. The required electric field is two point five times ten to the power of seven volts per meter. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 2.5 × 10⁷ volts per meter|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> Think about how enormous that is — two point five times ten to the seven volts per meter just to give a single electron one electron volt of energy. This is precisely why materials with large band gaps behave as insulators under ordinary voltages: the fields you'd need to push electrons across the gap simply aren't available in everyday conditions. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A ten centimeter slab of diamond has a band gap of about six electron volts. What battery voltage is needed to drive current through it?|id=ex-q-1>> Diamond's band gap — the energy gap between its highest filled band and the lowest empty band — is about six electron volts. The question is: how large a voltage would you actually need to push an electron across that gap through a real slab of material? To get an electron the energy it needs, the electric field inside the material has to be strong enough to supply six electron volts over the distance the electron travels. <<WRITE_STEP:Electric field required ~ 10^7 V/m  (to supply ~6 eV to an electron, same order as in copper)|id=ex-step-1-1>> From a companion example in the textbook, the electric field needed to supply six electron volts of energy to an electron is of the order of ten to the power of seven volts per meter. We assume the same value holds for diamond. Now we apply that field across our slab. <<WRITE_STEP:Slab thickness = ten centimeters = zero point one meters|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:V = E × d = (10^7 V/m) × (0.1 m) = 10^6 V|id=ex-step-1-3>> Voltage equals field strength times distance — ten to the power of seven volts per meter multiplied by zero point one meters — which gives ten to the power of six volts. <<PAUSE:short>> That is one million volts just to get a response from a single electron. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Required battery voltage ≈ 10^6 V  (one million volts) — diamond is a perfect insulator.|id=ex-ans-1>> This is why diamond is a perfect insulator: no ordinary battery could ever supply one million volts across a ten centimeter piece of diamond. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the thermal energy k T available to electrons at room temperature (three hundred kelvin)?|id=ex-q-1>> The textbook asks us to find k T at room temperature, which it defines as three hundred kelvin. This gives us a feel for the energy scale electrons are working with — and whether that's enough to jump a band gap. We evaluate k T by plugging in Boltzmann's constant and T equals three hundred kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:k T = (Boltzmann's constant) × 300 K|id=ex-step-1-1>> The product of those two numbers comes out to an energy in joules, but we convert to electron volts because that's the natural unit for band gaps in semiconductors. <<WRITE_STEP:k T ≈ 0.026 eV|id=ex-step-1-2>> And there's our answer. <<WRITE_ANSWER:At room temperature (three hundred kelvin), k T is approximately zero point zero two six electron volts.|id=ex-ans-1>> This is a crucially small number. Most semiconductor band gaps are on the order of one electron volt or more — meaning the thermal energy available at room temperature is roughly forty times smaller than a typical band gap. That's exactly why pure semiconductors conduct so poorly at room temperature: ordinary thermal jostling can only promote a tiny fraction of electrons across the gap. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why is silicon classified as a semiconductor, given its band gap?|id=ex-q-1>> The material in question is silicon, and the key fact the textbook gives us is that silicon has a band gap of one point one electron volts. Now, let's think about what that number means. <<WRITE_STEP:Band gap of silicon = one point one electron volts|id=ex-step-1-1>> The thermal energy available to electrons at room temperature is only around zero point zero two five electron volts — far less than the band gap of most insulators, which can be five electron volts or more. <<WRITE_STEP:Thermal energy at room temperature ≈ 0.025 eV  <<  band gap of insulators (~ 5 eV)|id=ex-step-1-2>> But silicon's band gap of one point one electron volts is comparatively small, so a modest amount of thermal energy is enough to push at least a few electrons across it. And that is exactly the conclusion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silicon (band gap = one point one electron volts) has a small enough gap that thermal energy at room temperature excites a few electrons across it — making silicon a semiconductor, not an insulator.|id=ex-ans-1>> Because the band gap of silicon is one point one electron volts, thermal excitation at room temperature is sufficient to promote a small but significant number of electrons into the conduction band, giving silicon its characteristic semiconducting behaviour. <<WRITE_KEY:Full band = no conduction; partially filled band = conductor|id=key-2>>So the answer to our diamond-versus-copper puzzle: copper's outermost band is half-filled — electrons roam freely. Diamond's filled band is separated from the empty band above by a huge gap of about five point five electron volts. Electrons are stuck. No current flows. <<POINT:upper-band-region>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So to summarise: when N atoms come together, each sharp atomic level fans out into a band of N levels. Whether that band is full or partly full — and how large the gap above it is — decides everything about whether a material is a metal, an insulator, or something in between. That in-between case is exactly what we will explore next: the semiconductor.

Now we apply that field across our slab. <<WRITE_STEP:Slab thickness = ten centimeters = zero point one meters|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:V = E × d = (10^7 V/m) × (0.1 m) = 10^6 V|id=ex-step-1-3>> Voltage equals field strength times distance — ten to the power of seven volts per meter multiplied by zero point one meters — which gives ten to the power of six volts. <<PAUSE:short>> That is one million volts just to get a response from a single electron. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Required battery voltage ≈ 10^6 V  (one million volts) — diamond is a perfect insulator.|id=ex-ans-1>> This is why diamond is a perfect insulator: no ordinary battery could ever supply one million volts across a ten centimeter piece of diamond. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the thermal energy k T available to electrons at room temperature (three hundred kelvin)?|id=ex-q-1>> The textbook asks us to find k T at room temperature, which it defines as three hundred kelvin. This gives us a feel for the energy scale electrons are working with — and whether that's enough to jump a band gap. We evaluate k T by plugging in Boltzmann's constant and T equals three hundred kelvin. <<WRITE_STEP:k T = (Boltzmann's constant) × 300 K|id=ex-step-1-1>> The product of those two numbers comes out to an energy in joules, but we convert to electron volts because that's the natural unit for band gaps in semiconductors. <<WRITE_STEP:k T ≈ 0.026 eV|id=ex-step-1-2>> And there's our answer. <<WRITE_ANSWER:At room temperature (three hundred kelvin), k T is approximately zero point zero two six electron volts.|id=ex-ans-1>> This is a crucially small number. Most semiconductor band gaps are on the order of one electron volt or more — meaning the thermal energy available at room temperature is roughly forty times smaller than a typical band gap. That's exactly why pure semiconductors conduct so poorly at room temperature: ordinary thermal jostling can only promote a tiny fraction of electrons across the gap. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why is silicon classified as a semiconductor, given its band gap?|id=ex-q-1>> The material in question is silicon, and the key fact the textbook gives us is that silicon has a band gap of one point one electron volts. Now, let's think about what that number means. <<WRITE_STEP:Band gap of silicon = one point one electron volts|id=ex-step-1-1>> The thermal energy available to electrons at room temperature is only around zero point zero two five electron volts — far less than the band gap of most insulators, which can be five electron volts or more. <<WRITE_STEP:Thermal energy at room temperature ≈ 0.025 eV  <<  band gap of insulators (~ 5 eV)|id=ex-step-1-2>> But silicon's band gap of one point one electron volts is comparatively small, so a modest amount of thermal energy is enough to push at least a few electrons across it. And that is exactly the conclusion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silicon (band gap = one point one electron volts) has a small enough gap that thermal energy at room temperature excites a few electrons across it — making silicon a semiconductor, not an insulator.|id=ex-ans-1>> Because the band gap of silicon is one point one electron volts, thermal excitation at room temperature is sufficient to promote a small but significant number of electrons into the conduction band, giving silicon its characteristic semiconducting behaviour. <<WRITE_KEY:Full band = no conduction; partially filled band = conductor|id=key-2>>So the answer to our diamond-versus-copper puzzle: copper's outermost band is half-filled — electrons roam freely. Diamond's filled band is separated from the empty band above by a huge gap of about five point five electron volts. Electrons are stuck. No current flows. <<POINT:upper-band-region>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So to summarise: when N atoms come together, each sharp atomic level fans out into a band of N levels. Whether that band is full or partly full — and how large the gap above it is — decides everything about whether a material is a metal, an insulator, or something in between. That in-between case is exactly what we will explore next: the semiconductor.

segments.narration_chapter: Here's something strange: silicon is an insulator at absolute zero — zero charge carriers, zero current. Heat it up just a little, and it starts conducting. How does warmth create electricity? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_3:silicon_lattice>> <<SECTION:Silicon's Covalent Lattice|id=sec-1>>Let's look inside silicon. Each silicon atom has four outer electrons, and it shares one with each of its four neighbours to form covalent bonds. <<WRITE_TEXT:Si: 4 outer electrons → 4 covalent bonds|id=text-1>>Every electron in every bond sits in the valence band — locked in place, unable to carry current. <<TRACE:si-atom-grid>> <<FOCUS:broken-bond-site>> Now, at room temperature, atoms are constantly jiggling — thermally vibrating. Occasionally, one of those vibrations is violent enough to give a valence electron the energy it needs to break free of its bond entirely. <<SECTION:The Energy Gap|id=sec-2>>How much energy does that electron need? For silicon, the gap between the valence band and the conduction band is one point one electron volts. <<WRITE_KEY:Silicon energy gap = 1.1 eV|id=key-1>>That gap is small enough that ordinary thermal energy — room-temperature heat — can occasionally bridge it. <<POINT:free-electron>> <<PAUSE:short>> The energy gap is the minimum energy an electron needs to jump from the valence band into the conduction band — for silicon that's one point one electron volts, for germanium it's zero point six eight electron volts. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E_{\text{gap}}(\text{Si}) = 1.1\,\text{eV}, \quad E_{\text{gap}}(\text{Ge}) = 0.68\,\text{eV}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Germanium's gap is even smaller — just zero point six eight electron volts — which is why germanium conducts more readily at the same temperature. <<WRITE_TEXT:Germanium gap = 0.68 eV|id=text-2>>The smaller the gap, the easier thermal energy can knock electrons free. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:broken-bond-site>> So the electron escapes — it's now in the conduction band, free to wander from nucleus to nucleus and carry current. But here's the question I want you to think about: what's left behind at the broken bond? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:hole-marker>> <<SECTION:The Hole|id=sec-3>>A vacancy. An empty spot where an electron used to be. And because the surrounding lattice is electrically neutral except for this missing negative charge, that vacancy behaves as if it has a positive charge. We call it a hole. <<WRITE_KEY:Broken bond → hole: a positive vacancy acting as a real charge carrier|id=key-2>> <<POINT:hole-marker>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now watch what happens next. A neighbouring electron — still in its own bond — can slip over and fill this vacancy. The vacancy then appears one bond over. Then another electron fills that, and the vacancy hops again. <<TRACE:hole-drift-arrow>> Even though it's always electrons that are actually moving, the vacancy — the hole — appears to drift in the opposite direction, as if a positive particle were flowing through the crystal. <<WRITE_TEXT:Hole drifts opposite to electron flow|id=text-3>>That's two charge carriers from one broken bond: one conduction electron, one hole. <<POINT:hole-drift-arrow>> <<POINT:hole-drift-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example straight from the chapter on semiconductors. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Phosphorus is doped into silicon at a proportion of one in ten to the power of six. By what factor does the conductivity increase?|id=ex-q-1>> We have phosphorus being introduced into silicon — and the proportion is just one phosphorus atom for every ten to the power of six silicon atoms. That is an almost unimaginably tiny amount of impurity. Now, you might expect such a minuscule proportion of phosphorus — one part in ten to the power of six — to have a negligible effect on the material. <<WRITE_STEP:Dopant proportion: 1 in 10^6 phosphorus atoms in silicon|id=ex-step-1-1>> But phosphorus is a donor impurity, meaning each phosphorus atom donates a free electron that silicon itself cannot provide. Even at this vanishingly small concentration, those extra free electrons dramatically change how easily current can flow through the material. And the result is remarkable. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Conductivity increases by a factor of about 10^6 — matching the doping proportion exactly!|id=ex-ans-1>> The conductivity increases by a factor of about ten to the power of six. So a proportion of one in ten to the power of six produces a conductivity boost of ten to the power of six. This is the key lesson about doping: semiconductors are extraordinarily sensitive to even trace amounts of impurity, and that sensitivity is exactly what makes them so useful in electronics. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How far below the conduction band is the impurity energy level for phosphorus in silicon?|id=ex-q-1>> We're looking at what happens when phosphorus is introduced as a donor impurity into silicon. The key question is: how much energy separates those extra donor electrons from the conduction band? When phosphorus atoms sit inside a silicon crystal, each one donates an extra electron that doesn't quite belong to any one bond. These electrons occupy what we call impurity levels — energy states that are created by the dopant, sitting just inside the gap. <<WRITE_STEP:Impurity: phosphorus in silicon → donor impurity levels form just below conduction band|id=ex-step-1-1>> The critical thing is just how close those levels are to the conduction band edge. The textbook tells us that for phosphorus in silicon, the impurity level sits only zero point zero four five electron volts below the conduction band. <<WRITE_STEP:E_gap (donor to conduction band) = 0.045 eV  (for P in Si)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Compare that to the full silicon band gap of about one point one electron volts — this impurity level is extremely close to the top. Room-temperature thermal energy, which is roughly zero point zero two five electron volts, is almost enough on its own to bridge that tiny gap. <<PAUSE:short>> So in practice, at room temperature, virtually all of the donor electrons are thermally excited up into the conduction band and are free to conduct. And so the answer is: the donor impurity level for phosphorus in silicon is just zero point zero four five electron volts below the conduction band — so close that ordinary thermal energy is sufficient to promote those electrons into the conduction band, making phosphorus-doped silicon an effective n-type conductor. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Impurity level for P in Si: 0.045 eV below the conduction band — thermal energy is sufficient to excite donor electrons into conduction|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're looking at aluminium as an impurity in silicon — a classic p-type dopant. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What energy is needed for a valence electron to fill the broken bond of an aluminium impurity in silicon, and what does this imply about the impurity energy level?|id=ex-q-1>> Now, aluminium has only three outer electrons, but silicon needs four bonds with each neighbour. So the aluminium atom leaves one bond broken — it simply doesn't have that fourth electron to contribute. The broken bond between the aluminium atom and its fourth silicon neighbour can be filled by a nearby valence electron — but only if that electron picks up a little extra energy. <<WRITE_STEP:Energy needed to fill broken bond ≈ 0.057 eV|id=ex-step-1-1>> That amount is about zero point zero five seven electron volts — a very small energy compared to the full band gap of silicon, which means this process happens quite readily at room temperature. When a valence electron jumps up to fill that broken bond, it leaves behind a vacancy in the valence band — we call that vacancy a hole. <<WRITE_STEP:Electron jumps to impurity level → hole created in valence band|id=ex-step-1-2>> So we say that acceptor impurity levels are created just above the valence band, sitting only zero point zero five seven electron volts above it for aluminium in silicon. <<PAUSE:short>> Because this gap is so tiny, valence electrons can easily make the jump, and the material ends up with an abundance of holes as its primary charge carriers. And the answer is: the impurity levels for aluminium in silicon lie zero point zero five seven electron volts above the valence band. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Acceptor impurity level = 0.057 eV above the valence band. Valence electrons jump up easily, creating holes in the valence band → p-type behaviour.|id=ex-ans-1>> This tiny energy separation is what makes aluminium an effective p-type dopant — holes are generated with very little thermal energy required. Here's an example straight from the chapter on semiconductors. The textbook highlights two common semiconductor materials — silicon and germanium — and tells us the size of their energy gaps, that is, the gap between the valence band and the conduction band. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What are the energy gaps for silicon and germanium, and what does this tell us about semiconductors?|id=ex-q-1>> For silicon, the energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band is one point one electron volts. For germanium, that same gap is zero point six eight electron volts. <<WRITE_STEP:Silicon energy gap = 1.1 eV|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Germanium energy gap = 0.68 eV|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now, compare these to a true insulator — diamond, for instance, has an energy gap of around five point five electron volts. The gaps for silicon and germanium are dramatically smaller, which means electrons don't need nearly as much energy to jump up into the conduction band and carry current. And that is the key takeaway. Because the energy gap is small — one point one electron volts for silicon and zero point six eight electron volts for germanium — these materials sit in a sweet spot: they're not good conductors at very low temperatures, but at room temperature, thermal energy is just enough to kick some electrons across the gap. That's what makes them semiconductors rather than insulators. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silicon: 1.1 eV gap | Germanium: 0.68 eV gap → small gap enables semiconducting behavior|id=ex-ans-1>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So the more thermal energy the silicon has, the more bonds break, the more electron-hole pairs are created, and the more current it can carry. That's why conductivity rises with temperature in a semiconductor — the exact opposite of a metal. To tie it all together: a semiconductor sits between conductor and insulator because its energy gap is small but not zero. Silicon's one point one electron volt gap means heat can bridge it, freeing electrons and creating holes — both carry charge, both matter.

segments.narration_chapter: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> If silicon is technically an insulator at absolute zero, why does it conduct electricity at room temperature — and can we actually count how many charge carriers are doing the job? It turns out we can, and the answer is a beautifully balanced story. <<FOCUS:valence-band>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_5:carrier_balance>> <<SECTION:Intrinsic Semiconductors|id=sec-1>>Picture the silicon crystal at room temperature. Every atom is vibrating. Most of the time, all bonding electrons stay put — but every so often, a vibrating atom gives one of those electrons just enough of a kick to break free. <<FOCUS:thermal-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Thermal energy → breaks covalent bond|id=text-1>>That freed electron shoots up into the conduction band, where it can wander and carry current. At the exact same moment, it leaves behind an empty spot in the bond — a hole — which acts like a positive charge carrier moving through the crystal. <<TRACE:thermal-arrow>> So for every free electron created, exactly one hole is created. They're born in pairs — electron-hole pairs. And this is happening constantly, all across the crystal. <<POINT:free-electron>> <<POINT:free-electron>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Free electron + hole = electron-hole pair|id=text-2>>But here's the question: does the crystal just keep filling up with more and more free electrons forever? <<POINT:conduction-band>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:recombination-arrow>> No — because the reverse process also happens. A free electron in the conduction band occasionally loses energy, drops back down, and fills a hole. The pair disappears. This is called recombination. <<TRACE:recombination-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Generation ⇌ Recombination → steady state|id=text-3>>Eventually, the rate of pair creation exactly balances the rate of recombination. A steady state is reached, and the number of electron-hole pairs settles at a nearly constant value. <<POINT:carrier-count-label>> <<FOCUS:carrier-count-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Silicon at 300 K: n ≈ p ≈ 7 × 10¹⁵ per cubic metre|id=key-1>>For silicon at room temperature — that's three hundred kelvin — this steady-state density is about seven times ten to the power fifteen electron-hole pairs per cubic metre. That's seven quadrillion per cubic metre. A staggeringly large number, yet still tiny compared to a metal. <<PAUSE:short>> For silicon at three hundred kelvin, the density of free electrons and holes are equal and settle at approximately seven times ten to the power fifteen per cubic metre. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n = p \approx 7 \times 10^{15} \, \text{m}^{-3}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:doping|to=0.7|duration=1800>> Now watch what happens when we add impurities — doping. Say we add a phosphorus atom, which has five outer electrons instead of four. Four of them form bonds with silicon neighbours, but the fifth is nearly free. <<FOCUS:free-electron>> <<WRITE_TEXT:n-type: extra electrons from donor atoms|id=text-4>>Those donor electrons jump easily into the conduction band. So suddenly we have many more free electrons — the electron density n shoots up dramatically. Here's an example from the chapter — Example forty-five point two. We have an n-type semiconductor, and we're asked to find its resistivity given some carrier data. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the resistivity of an n-type semiconductor given: nₑ = 8×10¹³ cm⁻³, nₕ = 5×10¹² cm⁻³, μₑ = 2.3×10⁴ cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹, μₕ = 100 cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹|id=ex-q-1>> The density of conduction electrons is eight times ten to the thirteen per cubic centimeter, which converts to eight times ten to the nineteen per cubic meter. The density of holes is five times ten to the twelve per cubic centimeter, converting to five times ten to the eighteen per cubic meter. The mobility of conduction electrons is two point three times ten to the four square centimeters per volt per second, which is two point three square meters per volt per second in SI units. And the mobility of holes is one hundred square centimeters per volt per second, which converts to ten to the negative two square meters per volt per second. When you dope a semiconductor, increasing one type of carrier forces the other type down — their product stays fixed for a given material at a given temperature. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n \times p = \text{constant}|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start by writing the conductivity formula. For a semiconductor with both conduction electrons and holes, sigma equals e times the quantity n-e times mu-e plus n-h times mu-h. <<WRITE_STEP:σ = e(nₑμₑ + nₕμₕ)|id=ex-step-1-1>> The charge of the electron e is one point six times ten to the negative nineteen coulombs. Now let's plug in all our SI values. <<WRITE_STEP:σ = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) × [(8 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³)(2.3 m² V⁻¹s⁻¹) + (5 × 10¹⁸ m⁻³)(10⁻² m² V⁻¹s⁻¹)]|id=ex-step-1-2>> Let's evaluate what's inside the brackets first. The electron contribution is eight times ten to the nineteen multiplied by two point three, which gives eighteen point four times ten to the nineteen. The hole contribution is five times ten to the eighteen multiplied by ten to the negative two, giving five times ten to the sixteen. That second term is much smaller, so the electron term dominates — this makes sense for an n-type semiconductor. Adding them together and multiplying by one point six times ten to the negative nineteen gives us a conductivity of approximately two point nine four coulombs per meter per volt per second. <<WRITE_STEP:σ ≈ 2.94 C m⁻¹ V⁻¹ s⁻¹|id=ex-step-1-3>> Finally, the resistivity rho equals one divided by sigma. <<WRITE_STEP:ρ = 1/σ|id=ex-step-1-4>> So we divide one by two point nine four to get the resistivity. <<PAUSE:short>> And the answer is approximately zero point three four ohm meters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ρ = 1/2.94 ≈ 0.34 Ω·m|id=ex-ans-1>> But here's the crucial twist: with so many extra electrons around, any hole that forms gets filled almost instantly. The hole density p plummets. The product n times p stays constant. <<POINT:np-product-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:np-product-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:n × p = constant for a given semiconductor|id=key-2>>This is the law of mass action for semiconductors. Boost the electrons with doping, and holes become rare. Boost the holes with p-type doping, and electrons become rare. The product never changes — it's fixed by the material and the temperature. <<PAUSE:short>>

It turns out we can, and the answer is a beautifully balanced story. <<FOCUS:valence-band>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:45_5:carrier_balance>> <<SECTION:Intrinsic Semiconductors|id=sec-1>>Picture the silicon crystal at room temperature. Every atom is vibrating. Most of the time, all bonding electrons stay put — but every so often, a vibrating atom gives one of those electrons just enough of a kick to break free. <<FOCUS:thermal-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Thermal energy → breaks covalent bond|id=text-1>>That freed electron shoots up into the conduction band, where it can wander and carry current. At the exact same moment, it leaves behind an empty spot in the bond — a hole — which acts like a positive charge carrier moving through the crystal. <<TRACE:thermal-arrow>> So for every free electron created, exactly one hole is created. They're born in pairs — electron-hole pairs. And this is happening constantly, all across the crystal. <<POINT:free-electron>> <<POINT:free-electron>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Free electron + hole = electron-hole pair|id=text-2>>But here's the question: does the crystal just keep filling up with more and more free electrons forever? <<POINT:conduction-band>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:recombination-arrow>> No — because the reverse process also happens. A free electron in the conduction band occasionally loses energy, drops back down, and fills a hole. The pair disappears. This is called recombination. <<TRACE:recombination-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Generation ⇌ Recombination → steady state|id=text-3>>Eventually, the rate of pair creation exactly balances the rate of recombination. A steady state is reached, and the number of electron-hole pairs settles at a nearly constant value. <<POINT:carrier-count-label>> <<FOCUS:carrier-count-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Silicon at 300 K: n ≈ p ≈ 7 × 10¹⁵ per cubic metre|id=key-1>>For silicon at room temperature — that's three hundred kelvin — this steady-state density is about seven times ten to the power fifteen electron-hole pairs per cubic metre. That's seven quadrillion per cubic metre. A staggeringly large number, yet still tiny compared to a metal. <<PAUSE:short>> For silicon at three hundred kelvin, the density of free electrons and holes are equal and settle at approximately seven times ten to the power fifteen per cubic metre. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n = p \approx 7 \times 10^{15} \, \text{m}^{-3}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:doping|to=0.7|duration=1800>> Now watch what happens when we add impurities — doping. Say we add a phosphorus atom, which has five outer electrons instead of four. Four of them form bonds with silicon neighbours, but the fifth is nearly free. <<FOCUS:free-electron>> <<WRITE_TEXT:n-type: extra electrons from donor atoms|id=text-4>>Those donor electrons jump easily into the conduction band. So suddenly we have many more free electrons — the electron density n shoots up dramatically. Here's an example from the chapter — Example forty-five point two. We have an n-type semiconductor, and we're asked to find its resistivity given some carrier data. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the resistivity of an n-type semiconductor given: nₑ = 8×10¹³ cm⁻³, nₕ = 5×10¹² cm⁻³, μₑ = 2.3×10⁴ cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹, μₕ = 100 cm² V⁻¹s⁻¹|id=ex-q-1>> The density of conduction electrons is eight times ten to the thirteen per cubic centimeter, which converts to eight times ten to the nineteen per cubic meter. The density of holes is five times ten to the twelve per cubic centimeter, converting to five times ten to the eighteen per cubic meter. The mobility of conduction electrons is two point three times ten to the four square centimeters per volt per second, which is two point three square meters per volt per second in SI units. And the mobility of holes is one hundred square centimeters per volt per second, which converts to ten to the negative two square meters per volt per second. When you dope a semiconductor, increasing one type of carrier forces the other type down — their product stays fixed for a given material at a given temperature. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n \times p = \text{constant}|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start by writing the conductivity formula. For a semiconductor with both conduction electrons and holes, sigma equals e times the quantity n-e times mu-e plus n-h times mu-h. <<WRITE_STEP:σ = e(nₑμₑ + nₕμₕ)|id=ex-step-1-1>> The charge of the electron e is one point six times ten to the negative nineteen coulombs. Now let's plug in all our SI values. <<WRITE_STEP:σ = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) × [(8 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³)(2.3 m² V⁻¹s⁻¹) + (5 × 10¹⁸ m⁻³)(10⁻² m² V⁻¹s⁻¹)]|id=ex-step-1-2>> Let's evaluate what's inside the brackets first. The electron contribution is eight times ten to the nineteen multiplied by two point three, which gives eighteen point four times ten to the nineteen. The hole contribution is five times ten to the eighteen multiplied by ten to the negative two, giving five times ten to the sixteen. That second term is much smaller, so the electron term dominates — this makes sense for an n-type semiconductor. Adding them together and multiplying by one point six times ten to the negative nineteen gives us a conductivity of approximately two point nine four coulombs per meter per volt per second. <<WRITE_STEP:σ ≈ 2.94 C m⁻¹ V⁻¹ s⁻¹|id=ex-step-1-3>> Finally, the resistivity rho equals one divided by sigma. <<WRITE_STEP:ρ = 1/σ|id=ex-step-1-4>> So we divide one by two point nine four to get the resistivity. <<PAUSE:short>> And the answer is approximately zero point three four ohm meters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ρ = 1/2.94 ≈ 0.34 Ω·m|id=ex-ans-1>> But here's the crucial twist: with so many extra electrons around, any hole that forms gets filled almost instantly. The hole density p plummets. The product n times p stays constant. <<POINT:np-product-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:np-product-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:n × p = constant for a given semiconductor|id=key-2>>This is the law of mass action for semiconductors. Boost the electrons with doping, and holes become rare. Boost the holes with p-type doping, and electrons become rare. The product never changes — it's fixed by the material and the temperature. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Heat up a metal wire and it resists more — that makes sense, right? Now heat up a semiconductor and something completely backwards happens: it actually gets BETTER at conducting. How can heat make something less resistive? <<FOCUS:band-gap-arrow>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:2_94 m:semiconductor_temp>> <<SECTION:Semiconductors vs Metals — Temperature Effect|id=sec-1>>To understand this, picture the energy landscape inside a semiconductor. Electrons sit in the valence band — a low-energy zone — and they'd love to jump up into the conduction band where they can move freely. But there's a gap in between, the band gap. <<FOCUS:electron-low-temp>> At low temperatures, almost no electrons have enough energy to leap that gap. So we have very few free carriers — barely any current can flow. Here's the key question: what changes when we crank up the temperature? <<POINT:electron-low-temp>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:temperature|to=90.0|from=10.0|duration=2500>> <<WRITE_KEY:More heat → more electron-hole pairs → lower resistivity|id=key-1>>Watch what happens as temperature rises — electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the gap. Every electron that jumps up leaves behind a hole in the valence band. We get electron-hole PAIRS, and the count of these pairs grows rapidly with temperature. <<PAUSE:short>> The number of electron-hole pairs grows with temperature in a very specific way — it scales with temperature to the power of three halves, multiplied by an exponential that depends on the band gap divided by the thermal energy. A bigger band gap means fewer pairs; a higher temperature means exponentially more. <<WRITE_EQUATION:n_{pairs} \propto T^{3/2}\, e^{-\Delta E / 2kT}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:electron-high-temp>> <<WRITE_TEXT:More carriers → conductivity up, resistivity DOWN|id=text-1>>Yes, thermal collisions do slow each carrier a little — just like in a metal. But that effect is tiny compared to the explosion in the NUMBER of carriers. So the net result: resistivity falls as temperature rises. The temperature coefficient is NEGATIVE for semiconductors — roughly negative zero point zero seven per kelvin for silicon. A metal does the exact opposite. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:p-region>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:semiconductors_and_semiconductor_devices:2_94 m:pn_junction>> <<SECTION:The p-n Junction|id=sec-2>>Now let's talk about what happens when we join two types of semiconductor side by side. On the left, p-type material — doped so it has an abundance of holes, positive charge carriers. On the right, n-type — doped so it has an abundance of free electrons. <<FOCUS:depletion-zone>> The moment these two sides touch, electrons from the n-side diffuse over and fill holes on the p-side. This creates a narrow zone right at the junction where all the carriers have cancelled out. We call it the depletion region. <<FOCUS:built-in-field-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Depletion region → built-in E field (n to p)|id=text-2>>Because electrons left the n-side, that side becomes positively charged. Because electrons arrived on the p-side, it becomes negatively charged. This sets up a built-in electric field pointing from n to p — it acts like an invisible wall that stops MORE carriers from crossing. So here's the big question: can we push current through a p-n junction, and does it matter which way we push? <<POINT:depletion-zone>> <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a p-n junction diode, and we need to find its approximate dynamic resistance at two different forward bias voltages. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the dynamic resistance of a p-n junction at (a) forward bias of one volt, and (b) forward bias of two volts.|id=ex-q-1>> Remember, dynamic resistance is defined as R equals delta V divided by delta i — that is, a small change in voltage divided by the corresponding small change in current. Let's tackle part a first. At a forward bias of one volt, the current through the diode is ten milliamperes. Now we look at a nearby point on the characteristic curve: at one point two volts, the current is fifteen milliamperes. So the change in voltage is zero point two volts, and the change in current is five milliamperes. <<WRITE_STEP:(a) At V = 1 V, i = 10 mA; at V = 1.2 V, i = 15 mA|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:ΔV = 0.2 V, Δi = 5 mA|id=ex-step-1-2>> Plugging into the formula, R equals delta V divided by delta i equals zero point two volts divided by five milliamperes. <<WRITE_STEP:R = ΔV / Δi = 0.2 V / 5 mA = 40 Ω|id=ex-step-1-3>> That gives us a dynamic resistance of forty ohms at one volt forward bias. Notice this is quite a significant resistance — we're still in the lower region of the forward bias curve where the diode hasn't fully turned on. Now for part b, at a higher forward bias of two volts, the current has jumped dramatically to four hundred milliamperes. At two point one volts, the current is eight hundred milliamperes. So the change in voltage is zero point one volts, and the change in current is four hundred milliamperes — a huge swing for a tiny voltage step! <<WRITE_STEP:(b) At V = 2 V, i = 400 mA; at V = 2.1 V, i = 800 mA|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:ΔV = 0.1 V, Δi = 400 mA|id=ex-step-1-5>> Applying the formula again, R equals zero point one volts divided by four hundred milliamperes. <<WRITE_STEP:R = ΔV / Δi = 0.1 V / 400 mA = 0.25 Ω|id=ex-step-1-6>> That gives us just zero point two five ohms — a tiny fraction of what we got in part a. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:(a) Dynamic resistance at 1 V forward bias = 40 Ω  |  (b) Dynamic resistance at 2 V forward bias = 0.25 Ω|id=ex-ans-1>> And this beautifully illustrates the key lesson: as forward bias increases and the diode conducts more heavily, the dynamic resistance drops dramatically — from forty ohms all the way down to zero point two five ohms — because the curve gets much steeper and a small voltage change produces a very large change in current. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Given a mobility value of two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb to the power of negative one, find the resulting resistivity.|id=ex-q-1>> We're given a mobility — that's the drift speed per unit electric field per unit charge — of two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb, raised to the negative one power. Our job is to figure out the resistivity that comes from that value. Now, resistivity is inversely related to the mobility. So we take the reciprocal of our mobility value. <<WRITE_STEP:rho = 1 / (2.94 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ C⁻¹)|id=ex-step-1-1>> In other words, we flip the two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb quantity to get our resistivity. Carrying out that division gives us our result. <<WRITE_ANSWER:rho ≈ 0.34 ohm-meters|id=ex-ans-1>> The resulting resistivity is approximately zero point three four ohm-meters. So a mobility of two point nine four meters squared per volt-second per coulomb to the negative one gives a resistivity of about zero point three four ohm-meters. Here's an example from the chapter. We're looking at silicon, a semiconductor material, and we want to identify its temperature coefficient of resistivity. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the average temperature coefficient of resistivity for silicon?|id=ex-q-1>> Recall that for metals the temperature coefficient of resistivity is positive — meaning resistivity goes up with temperature. But silicon is a semiconductor, and semiconductors behave differently. As temperature rises, more charge carriers become available, so resistivity actually decreases. This means the coefficient must be negative. <<WRITE_STEP:Silicon is a semiconductor → resistivity decreases as temperature increases|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Therefore: temperature coefficient of resistivity α < 0|id=ex-step-1-2>> And indeed, the textbook confirms this. The average value of the temperature coefficient of resistivity for silicon is negative zero point zero seven per kelvin. <<PAUSE:short>> That negative sign is the key result — it tells us definitively that silicon's resistivity goes down as temperature goes up, which is the hallmark of a semiconductor. <<WRITE_ANSWER:α (silicon) = negative zero point zero seven per kelvin|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on p-n junction rectifier circuits. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In a rectifier circuit, the p-n junction is forward biased. Given that the junction resistance is much less than the load resistance R, what is the current through the load?|id=ex-q-3>> We have a sinusoidal source voltage V equal to V zero times sine of omega t plus phi, and the key condition is that in forward bias, the junction resistance is much, much less than the load resistance R. Now, because the junction resistance is negligible compared to R in forward bias, we can drop the junction resistance from the total resistance in the circuit. <<WRITE_STEP:In forward bias: R_junction << R|id=ex-step-3-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:So total resistance ≈ R (junction resistance is negligible)|id=ex-step-3-2>> This approximation holds precisely because the junction resistance is so much smaller than R that it contributes almost nothing to the overall opposition to current flow. And so the current through the load is simply the source voltage divided by R. <<PAUSE:short>> Using Ohm's law, i is approximately V zero divided by R, times sine of omega t plus phi. <<WRITE_ANSWER:i ≈ V zero divided by R, times sine of omega t plus phi|id=ex-ans-3>> That is the answer — because junction resistance is negligible compared to R, the full source voltage effectively appears across the load, and the current follows that same sinusoidal shape, scaled by one over R. Here's an example from the chapter on LEDs and visible light. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Under what conditions does an LED emit visible light, and which semiconductor materials can produce it?|id=ex-q-1>> When an electron and a hole recombine inside an LED, they release energy as a photon. The key question is: does that photon's wavelength fall inside the visible range? The textbook tells us the visible range runs from three hundred eighty nanometers all the way up to seven hundred eighty nanometers — anything outside that window, and our eyes simply cannot see it. Now, not every semiconductor hits that window. <<WRITE_STEP:Silicon and germanium → photon wavelengths in the infrared (beyond 780 nm) → NOT visible|id=ex-step-1-1>> Silicon and germanium are the workhorses of electronics, but the photon wavelengths they produce by electron-hole recombination fall in the infrared range — beyond seven hundred eighty nanometers. So even though they are emitting photons, those photons are invisible to us. A silicon or germanium LED is not a useful light source for anything we can see with our eyes. To get visible light, we need materials whose recombination energy lands a photon between three hundred eighty and seven hundred eighty nanometers. <<WRITE_STEP:Compound semiconductors, e.g. gallium arsenide, indium phosphide → photon wavelengths inside 380 nm – 780 nm → visible light emitted|id=ex-step-1-2>> Compounds like gallium arsenide and indium phosphide have the right bandgap energies to do exactly that. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Visible LEDs require photon wavelength in 380 nm – 780 nm; achievable with compounds such as gallium arsenide or indium phosphide — NOT with silicon or germanium (infrared)|id=ex-ans-1>> So the answer is: an LED glows visibly only when its semiconductor material produces photons in the three-hundred-eighty to seven-hundred-eighty nanometer range, and that rules out silicon and germanium entirely — you need compound materials like gallium arsenide or indium phosphide to build a working visible-light LED. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:forward-bias-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:p-n junction = one-way gate; forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks|id=key-2>>Absolutely — direction is everything. Forward bias: connect positive to the p-side and negative to the n-side, and your external voltage OPPOSES the built-in field. The depletion region shrinks, the barrier falls, and current flows freely. Reverse bias: flip it, the depletion region WIDENS, the barrier grows, and almost no current gets through. The junction is a one-way gate. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So to wrap it up — semiconductors are fascinating precisely because they BREAK the rules we learned for metals. Heat them up and they conduct better, because more carriers are born. Join p-type to n-type and you get a junction that only lets current pass one way — and that's the foundation of every diode, every transistor, every chip in your phone. <<PAUSE:short>>

To get visible light, we need materials whose recombination energy lands a photon between three hundred eighty and seven hundred eighty nanometers. <<WRITE_STEP:Compound semiconductors, e.g. gallium arsenide, indium phosphide → photon wavelengths inside 380 nm – 780 nm → visible light emitted|id=ex-step-1-2>> Compounds like gallium arsenide and indium phosphide have the right bandgap energies to do exactly that. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Visible LEDs require photon wavelength in 380 nm – 780 nm; achievable with compounds such as gallium arsenide or indium phosphide — NOT with silicon or germanium (infrared)|id=ex-ans-1>> So the answer is: an LED glows visibly only when its semiconductor material produces photons in the three-hundred-eighty to seven-hundred-eighty nanometer range, and that rules out silicon and germanium entirely — you need compound materials like gallium arsenide or indium phosphide to build a working visible-light LED. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:forward-bias-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:p-n junction = one-way gate; forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks|id=key-2>>Absolutely — direction is everything. Forward bias: connect positive to the p-side and negative to the n-side, and your external voltage OPPOSES the built-in field. The depletion region shrinks, the barrier falls, and current flows freely. Reverse bias: flip it, the depletion region WIDENS, the barrier grows, and almost no current gets through.
